aarau: Aarau lies on the Swiss Plateau, in the valley of the Aare, on the river's right bank and at the southern foot of the Jura Mountains. It is 58 kilometres south of Basel and 65 kilometres northeast of Bern, and its municipality borders the canton of Solothurn to the west. The old city stands on a rocky outcrop at a narrowing of the valley, with newer districts to the south and east. The name goes back to Arowe, first recorded in 1248, and comes, like the name of the Aare, from the German word Au, meaning floodplain.

A few Neolithic artefacts have been found, and ruins of a Bronze Age settlement of about 1000 BCE were excavated near the present railway station. The Roman road between Salodurum (Solothurn) and Vindonissa passed through the area, and in 1976 divers found part of a seven-metre-wide wooden bridge of late Roman times in the Aare. The counts of Kyburg founded the town around 1240. It is first mentioned in 1248, and the first mention of a city-sized settlement dates to 1256.

The Kyburg line died out in 1273, and Agnes of Kyburg, who had no male relations, sold the family's lands to King Rudolf I von Habsburg, who granted Aarau its city rights in 1283. In the 14th century the town was extended in two stages and a second wall was built, with a deep ditch, now the street called Graben, separating it from its suburb. The buildings of the old town mostly come from the 16th century, when nearly all the medieval buildings were replaced or enlarged, and its growth within the walls ended in the 18th century. The Schlössli, founded shortly after 1200, is the oldest building, and the city hall was built around the Rore tower in 1515.

Aarau is the capital of the canton of Aargau and of the district of Aarau, and the largest town in the canton. It is German-speaking and predominantly Protestant, and the cantonal government is its largest employer. It is known for its painted gables, and its old town, the cantonal library, the state archive and the art museum are listed as heritage sites of national significance. The Kern & Co. firm, founded in 1819, made geodetic instruments there until it closed in 1991. Its population peaked at 17,045 in 1960, more than five times that of 1800.
aargau: Aargau is one of the most northerly cantons of Switzerland and takes its name from the lower course of the Aare River, Aar-gau meaning 'Aare province'. It borders Germany to the north, with the Rhine forming the boundary, and the cantons of Basel-Landschaft, Solothurn and Bern to the west, Lucerne to the south, and Zürich and Zug to the east. Its area is 1,404 square kilometres. It forms part of the Swiss Plateau, north of the Alps and east of the Jura, and is one of the least mountainous cantons. The Aare, the Reuss and the Rhine are its large rivers, and it has hot sulphur springs at Baden and Schinznach-Bad and saline springs at Rheinfelden.

The area was controlled by the Helvetians, a tribe of Celts, as far back as 200 BCE. It was later occupied by the Romans, who built a major settlement, Vindonissa, near the present Brugg, and by the 6th century by the Franks. The Old High German name Argowe is first clearly attested, as Argue, in 795, and described a territory only loosely equivalent to the modern canton. It stretched between the Aare and the Reuss and took in parts of the present cantons of Bern, Solothurn, Basel-Landschaft, Lucerne, Obwalden and Nidwalden, but not the Baden district east of the Reuss, which belonged to Zürichgau.

Within the Frankish Empire the area was a disputed border region between the duchies of Alamannia and Burgundy. A line of the von Wetterau, the Conradines, held the countship of Aargau intermittently from 750 until about 1030. When the Holy Roman Empire formed in the later 10th century this became its sparsely settled outer border. By about 1200 most of the region was controlled by the ducal house of Zähringen and the comital houses of Habsburg and Kyburg. The canton's flag and arms date to 1803, an original design by Samuel Ringier-Seelmatter.

Aargau is one of the 26 cantons of the Swiss Confederation and has eleven districts. Its capital is Aarau, on its western border. It is one of the most densely populated regions of Switzerland and its population speaks mainly German. Its farmland is among the most fertile in the country, and three of Switzerland's five nuclear power plants and many hydroelectric plants stand in the canton, which is often called the energy canton. Near Brugg lie the ruined castle of Habsburg, the old convent of Königsfelden with its painted medieval glass, and the remains of Vindonissa at Windisch.
abbeville: Abbeville lies on the river Somme in northern France, 20 km from the river's modern mouth in the English Channel, about 45 km northwest of Amiens and roughly 200 km from Paris. Most of the town stands on the east bank and on an island, at the head of the Abbeville Canal. In the medieval period it was the lowest crossing point on the Somme, and Edward III's army crossed nearby shortly before the Battle of Crécy in 1346. It is the historical capital of the County of Ponthieu.

The subsoil holds many remains of the Pleistocene, and their discovery helped found prehistory as a science. Jacques Boucher de Perthes found handaxes near Abbeville from 1838 and in 1846 published the first description pointing out that the stones had been chipped deliberately by early humans to form a tool. They were known as Abbevillian handaxes, though that term is becoming obsolete. The Romans occupied the place and named it Abbatis Villa, and the modern name means villa of the abbé, as it once depended on the Abbey of Saint-Riquier. Abbeville prided itself on never having been taken, was called Abbeville la pucelle, and received many privileges from the Capetian kings in reward for its loyalty.

In 1665 the Van Robais family founded the Manufacture Royale des Rames, making linens and tablecloths. The cloth trade declined after the revocation of the Edict of Nantes and the departure of Protestants, and the closing of the river port because of silt also hurt the economy. In the 18th century, according to Voltaire's account, the judges of Abbeville condemned the Chevalier de La Barre to torture and a slow death for impious songs and for passing a procession without removing his hat. The German army bombed the town almost to rubble in one night in the early days of the Second World War.

Abbeville is a commune in the Somme department of the Hauts-de-France region and a sub-prefecture of the department. Much of the town is modern and rebuilt. The Collegiate Church of Saint-Vulfran, begun in 1488 and continued in the 16th and 17th centuries, has a facade that is a masterpiece of flamboyant Gothic architecture, flanked by two towers, and was classified as a historical monument in 1840. The Boucher de Perthes Museum shows some of the stone tools, and the municipal library keeps 972 manuscripts, among them a Carolingian Gospel book dated 790–800.
abellinum: Before the Roman conquest, the ancient Abellinum was a centre of the Samnite Hirpini on the Civita hill, about 4 km outside the current town of Avellino, in what is now Atripalda. It could correspond to the ancient Velecha, known from coins found in the area. The later Roman town lay on the left bank of the river Sabato.

The Romans conquered Abellinum in 293 BCE, and over the following centuries it changed name several times: Veneria, Livia, Augusta, Alexandriana and Abellinatium. A true Roman town, however, was built only after Lucius Cornelius Sulla's conquest in the civil wars in 89 BCE. He razed the old site and in 82 BCE founded the colony Veneria Abellinatium. The new city had massive walls and an orthogonal Hippodamian layout. In 7 CE Augustus renamed it Livia Augusta, for his wife Livia Drusilla, who owned the territory between Abellinum and Aeclanum. In the 3rd century Alexander Severus expanded the colony with a massive immigration of oriental settlers, which helped to spread Levantine cults such as Sol Invictus in the territory.

Economic crises in the 3rd and 4th centuries, violent earthquakes in 346 and disastrous volcanic eruptions in 472 followed. The town was Christianised around 500 and became an episcopal seat. The Goths invaded between 535 and 555, and after the Lombard conquest of southern Italy the ancient city was abandoned in 568, though historians dispute whether completely or partly. A new settlement grew on the Terra hill, where modern Avellino stands.

The ruins of Abellinum lie near the village of Atripalda, 4 km east of Avellino. They include the forum, faced by temples, baths, parts of the Serino aqueduct and a patrician domus, as well as an amphitheatre. Avellino itself is the capital of its province in Campania, with 51,819 inhabitants, about 47 km east of Naples.
abgaal: The Abgaal belong to the Mudulood, one of the divisions of the Hiraab, with the Habar Gidir, Sheekhaal and Duduble. The clan is regarded as relatively young, its founder dating from the 1500s. A tradition recorded by the Italian scholar Enrico Cerulli makes the founder, Ali Isman, the son of Osman Darandolle of the Hiraab and of Faduma Sarjeele, a woman of the Gareen house that headed the Ajuran Sultanate.

According to the story, Faduma's father was warned that the boy's descendants would drive out his own and tried to poison him, but the mother drank the poison by mistake. The boy hid behind a camel and called the camels his grandfather, whence the name Abgaal, camel-grandfather. Cerulli read the story as a memory of fighting between Abgaal pastoral nomads coming from the north and the Ajuran.

Clan traditions say that the Abgaal Darandoolle began to arrive in the hinterland of Mogadishu in the sixteenth century, while the Muzaffar dynasty ruled the town, and manuscripts from Mogadishu record Abgaal nomads in the interior at about the same time. Towards the end of the seventeenth century an imam of Abgaal descent settled in the Shangaani quarter. His lineage, the Yaaquub, intermarried with merchant families of Yemeni origin and became known in the trade between the coast and the interior, and by the 1700s it ruled most of the town.

Traditions of the fall of the Ajuran speak of heavy taxes and of a quarrel over watering rights, after which the Darandoolle killed the Ajuran imam at a well called Ceel Cawl. According to oral tradition as reported by Lee Cassanelli, the Hiraab Imamate that followed was an alliance of related groups that ruled from the Shabelle valley to the arid lands of Mudug for at least two centuries. Mogadishu was its capital, and the port of Hobyo its commercial centre.

The Abgaal are divided into three main branches: the Harti, the eldest, the Wacbudhan and the Waceysle, the youngest. The imam of the Mudulood and of the Hiraab traditionally comes from the Abgaal, from the Owbakar sub-clan, while the ugaas of the Mudulood comes from the Reer Ugaas sub-clan. Mogadishu is regarded as Abgaal territory, and they form the majority of its population. Three presidents of Somalia, Ali Mahdi Muhammad, Sharif Sheikh Ahmed and Hassan Sheikh Mohamud, have been Abgaal, as was Daud Abdulle Hirsi, the first commander-in-chief of the Somali National Army.
abraham-lincoln: Abraham Lincoln was born on 12 February 1809 in a one-room log cabin in Kentucky, the second child of Thomas Lincoln and Nancy Hanks Lincoln, and was raised on farms near Hodgenville. His father bought several farms but could not secure clear titles to any, and in 1816 the family moved to Indiana, where land titles were more reliable. His parents belonged to a Separate Baptist church whose members largely opposed slavery. His mother died of milk sickness on 5 October 1818, and his father married Sarah Bush Johnston the following year; Lincoln became close to his stepmother. He married Mary Todd on 4 November 1842.

Lincoln served four terms in the Illinois House of Representatives from 1834, as a Whig and supporter of Henry Clay, and championed the Illinois and Michigan Canal. He won election to the U.S. House of Representatives in 1846 and served from 1847 to 1849. The Kansas–Nebraska Act of 1854, proposed by Senator Stephen A. Douglas, brought him back into political life. His Peoria Speech of October 1854 opposed slavery, and he became a leader of the new Republican Party. He reached a national audience in the 1858 Senate campaign debates with Douglas and won the 1860 presidential election.

Secession followed. South Carolina adopted an ordinance of secession on 20 December 1860, and six other states had followed by 1 February 1861, forming the Confederate States of America. Lincoln refused to recognise the Confederacy and declared secession illegal. He closely supervised the Union's strategy, including the choice of generals and a naval blockade of Southern ports. On 1 January 1863 he issued the Emancipation Proclamation, declaring slaves in states 'in rebellion' to be free. He delivered the Gettysburg Address on 19 November 1863, and he promoted the Thirteenth Amendment, which abolished chattel slavery in 1865.

On the evening of 14 April 1865, five days after the Confederate surrender at Appomattox, Lincoln attended the play Our American Cousin at Ford's Theatre in Washington. John Wilkes Booth, an actor and Confederate spy, entered his box at 10:15 pm and shot him in the back of the head. Lincoln was taken to the Petersen House across the street and died at 7:22 am on 15 April. He was the first U.S. president to be assassinated. His body lay in state in the White House and the Capitol, then travelled by funeral train to Springfield, Illinois, where crowds gathered along the route. The Lincoln Memorial on the National Mall was dedicated in 1922.
abu-hanifa: Abu Hanifa came from Central Asia, though sources disagree on his birthplace, naming Kufa (the majority view), Kabul, Anbar, Nasa or Termez. They agree that he was born under the Umayyad Caliphate but differ on the year: 699 CE, held by the majority of classical scholarship, or 696, 689 or 680. His first name was Nu'man. He was born at least 60 years after the death of Muhammad, when some of the first generation of Muslims were still alive.

In his youth Abu Hanifa travelled to the Hejaz and studied in Mecca and Medina, and he later became established as a leading religious authority in Kufa. One of his main teachers there was Hammad ibn Abi Sulayman. He never held an official post as qadi. He kept an independent position toward political authority and was punished and imprisoned under both the Umayyads and the Abbasids because of his views and his refusal to accept the office of qadi in Kufa. He died in prison in Baghdad in 767 (AH 150).

The scholar Yusuf ibn Abd al-Rahman al-Mizzi listed 97 hadith scholars among his students, and Badr al-Din al-Ayni named another 260 who studied hadith and fiqh with him. His two best-known students were Abu Yusuf, who served as the first chief justice in the Muslim world, and Muhammad al-Shaybani, who taught the founder of the Shafi'i school, al-Shafi'i.

Abu Hanifa derived Islamic law, in order of preference, from the Qur'an, the authentic narrations of Muhammad known as hadith, the consensus of the Muslim community (ijma'), analogical reasoning (qiyas), juristic discretion (istihsan) and local custom ('urf). Modern scholarship regards him as the first to formally adopt analogical reasoning as part of Islamic law. Because Ali had moved the Islamic capital to Kufa and many first-generation Muslims settled there, the school came to be known as the Kufan or Iraqi school.

His school, the Hanafi, remains the most widely practised of the Sunni schools. Abu Hanifa received the honorific al-Imam al-A'zam, the highly venerated Imam. His tomb, surmounted by a dome erected by admirers in 1066, is still a shrine for pilgrims; the Ottoman ruler Suleiman restored it in 1535 after the Ottoman conquest of Baghdad.
abu-simbel: Abu Simbel lies on the western bank of Lake Nasser in the Aswan Governorate of Upper Egypt, near the border with Sudan, about 230 km southwest of Aswan. The temples stand at the Second Nile Cataract, the border between Lower Nubia and Upper Nubia. Nubia was a major source of gold and other precious trade goods and was controlled by Egypt, so it mattered greatly to the Egyptians.

Ramesses II carried out an extensive building programme in Egypt and Nubia. He built several grand temples in Nubia in order to impress upon the Nubians Egypt's might and to Egyptianize the people of Nubia. Work at Abu Simbel began in about 1264 BCE and lasted for about 20 years, until 1244 BCE. The complex was known as the Temple of Ramesses, Beloved by Amun. It has two temples: the Great Temple, dedicated to Ra-Horakhty, Ptah and Amun and to the deified Ramesses himself, and the Small Temple, dedicated to the goddess Hathor, personified by his chief wife Nefertari.

Over time the temples fell into disuse and a sand dune came to cover most of the Great Temple. By the 6th century BCE the sand already covered the statues of the main temple up to their knees. The site remained unknown to Europeans until March 1813, when the Swiss researcher Johann Ludwig Burckhardt found the small temple and the top frieze of the main temple.

The Great Temple is entered between four seated statues of Ramesses II, each 20 m high, with smaller figures of his family beside his legs. The facade behind them is 33 m high and 38 m wide. The complex was moved in 1968 to higher ground, under an artificial hill, to keep it from being submerged by Lake Nasser, within the International Campaign to Save the Monuments of Nubia. Abu Simbel is part of the UNESCO World Heritage Site known as the Nubian Monuments, and is open to visitors.
abu-tahir-al-jannabi: Abu Tahir Sulayman was an Arabized Persian, born in June or July 906 at Ganaveh on the coast of Fars. His father, Abu Sa'id, a tribal leader taught by Hamdan Qarmat of Kufa, had begun the militarization of the Qarmatians.

Most Arabic sources agree that Abu Sa'id named his eldest son, Abu'l-Qasim Sa'id, as heir and that Abu Tahir revolted against him and usurped power. Another tradition, reported by the Kufan anti-Isma'ili polemicist Ibn Rizam, holds that Sa'id was only a regent and handed over power in 917/918, when his brother was barely ten. It is likely that power was nominally shared among all the sons, with Abu Tahir dominant. Abu'l-Qasim was not executed and lived until 972.

In 926 he led his army as far north as Kufa and made the Abbasids pay large sums for him to leave. On his return he built palaces at Ahsa and declared it his permanent capital. In 928 Caliph al-Muqtadir sent against him the generals Yusuf ibn Abi'l-Saj, Mu'nis al-Muzaffar and Harun, who were beaten and driven back to Baghdad.

At Mecca in 930 he was at first refused entry, invoked the right of all Muslims to enter and swore that he came in peace. Once inside, his men rode into the Masjid al-Haram, massacred the pilgrims, set fire to the Kaaba and threw bodies into the Zamzam Well. The attack was believed to be meant to prompt the appearance of the Mahdi and followed millenarian excitement over the conjunction of Saturn and Jupiter in 928.

The Mahdi he recognised in 931, Abu'l-Fadl al-Isfahani, a prisoner who claimed descent from the Sasanian kings, restored the veneration of fire, burned religious books and had members of Bahrayn's notable families executed. In one account Abu Tahir's mother exposed him and his brother Sa'id killed him after eighty days; in others Abu Tahir denounced him as a false Mahdi and had him executed.

Abu Tahir took back control of the state and resumed his attacks on pilgrims crossing Arabia. He rejected the attempts of both the Abbasids and the Fatimids to persuade him to return the Black Stone. He died of smallpox in 944, aged about 38, and was succeeded by his three surviving sons and his nephews. According to the historian al-Juwayni the stone came back in 951, thrown in a sack into the Great Mosque of Kufa with a note: "By command we took it, and by command we have brought it back." Its removal had broken it into seven pieces.
acapulco: Acapulco lies on the Pacific coast of Mexico in the state of Guerrero, 380 km south of Mexico City, on a deep, semicircular bay. The municipality is 40 percent mountainous, 40 percent semi-flat and 20 percent flat, with elevations from sea level to 1,699 metres. The climate is tropical wet and dry, and Pacific hurricanes and tropical storms are a threat from May through November. The name comes from the Nahuatl Aca-pol-co, meaning where the reeds were destroyed or washed away, or at the big reeds, which inspired the city's seal, a glyph of two hands breaking reeds.

By the 8th century a small culture existed around the bay, first dominated by the Olmecs, who had two sites there, and then by others, including Teotihuacan and later Maya influence. In the 11th century Nahua migrants, ancestors of the Aztecs, came through. In the later 15th century, after four years of fighting, Acapulco became part of the Aztec Empire under Ahuizotl, but only transitorily: the Yopis, who controlled the territory, kept defending it until the Spanish arrived in the 1520s.

Europeans are said to have found the bay in one of two ways. Either explorers sent by Hernán Cortés subdued the area after 1523 and Captain Saavedra Cerón was authorised to found a settlement, or a small ship under Santiago Guevara found it on 13 December 1526.

Acapulco is a port of call for shipping and cruise lines running between Panama and San Francisco and the largest city of Guerrero. It rose to prominence between the 1940s and the 1960s as one of Mexico's oldest beach resorts. It was the eastern end of the trans-Pacific sailing route to Manila, then in a Spanish colony.
achilles: In Greek myth Achilles was the son of Thetis, a Nereid, and Peleus, king of the Myrmidons. According to one account, Zeus and Poseidon had both courted Thetis until Prometheus warned Zeus of a prophecy that she would bear a son greater than his father, and the two gods had her wed Peleus. Achilles was raised in Phthia with his companion Patroclus and educated by the centaur Chiron.

The story that Thetis dipped him in the river Styx, leaving him vulnerable only at the heel, comes from the Achilleid of Statius, written in the first century CE. No source before Statius mentions general invulnerability: in the Iliad Achilles is wounded at the elbow.

According to the Iliad, Achilles came to Troy with 50 ships, each carrying 50 Myrmidons. On the way he wounded King Telephus of Mysia, a wound that would not heal until Achilles healed it, as an oracle had said. His most notable feat was the slaying of the Trojan prince Hector outside the gates of Troy.

The Iliad does not present his death, but other sources agree that Paris killed him near the end of the war with an arrow. His tomb in the Troad was venerated through antiquity by Thessalians, by Persian expeditionary forces, by Alexander the Great and by the emperor Caracalla. Dedications from Greek colonies on the Black Sea attest a heroic cult from the sixth century BCE, and in the third century CE stelae at Olbia name an Achilles Pontarches, invoked as protector of the city. Aeschylus wrote a trilogy about him, of which only fragments survive.
acropolis-of-athens: The Acropolis is a flat-topped rock that rises 150 metres above sea level in the city of Athens and has a surface of about 3 hectares. It is a klippe made of two rock units: the soft reddish Athens schist and the overlying Acropolis limestone, thrust over it by tectonic forces. The limestone is unstable and prone to rock slides. The marble of its buildings came from the quarries of Mount Pentelicus, northeast of the city. In ancient times the hill was also called Cecropia, after the first Athenian king Cecrops.

Habitation of the hill is evidenced as early as the 4th millennium BCE. A Mycenaean megaron palace probably stood there in the late Bronze Age, with a Cyclopean wall 760 metres long. Athena Polias had a temple, the Hekatompedon, built between 570 and 550 BCE. Around 500 BCE it was dismantled for a grander building, the Older Parthenon, which was still unfinished when the Persians sacked the city in 480 BCE. The Athenians built parts of it into the new northern wall, where they can still be seen.

Under Pericles, in the so-called Golden Age (460–430 BCE), the Parthenon and other temples were rebuilt, with the sculptor Phidias and the architects Ictinus and Callicrates responsible. Mnesicles began the Propylaea in 437 BCE, and the Erechtheion was built between 421 and 406 BCE. In the Byzantine period the Parthenon served as a church of the Virgin Mary. In 1687, during the Morean War, a Venetian bombardment hit the gunpowder the Ottomans kept in the Parthenon, and the explosion severely damaged it.

After Greek independence most Byzantine, Frankish and Ottoman additions were cleared from the site. The Parthenon mosque was demolished in 1843. The Acropolis Restoration Project, begun in 1975, reassembled original fragments with titanium dowels and used new Pentelic marble sparingly. The Acropolis Museum stands on the southern slope, 280 metres from the Parthenon.

In antiquity the Great Panathenaea, held every four years, ended with a procession to the Acropolis, where a new robe was placed on the statue of Athena. Since at least the mid-18th century the Acropolis has often been invoked as a symbol of the Greek legacy and of classical Greece.
aden: Aden lies on the north coast of the Gulf of Aden, near the eastern approach to the Red Sea and about 170 km east of the Strait of Bab al-Mandab, which makes it a gateway between the Red Sea and the Arabian Sea. The highlands of Jabal Shamsan rise in the south, with peaks above 500 metres, and like the rest of Yemen's highlands they are of volcanic origin. Aden encloses the eastern side of a vast natural harbour that forms the modern port.

The Greeks called Aden Arabia Emporion, the Arabian trading port, and in the 1st century BCE it was known as Eudaemon, a transshipping point for the Red Sea trade. According to the Periplus of the Erythraean Sea, it fell on hard times in the 1st century CE when ships began to cross directly to India. The Book of Ezekiel names Aden among the merchants of Sheba.

The British Empire held the city from 1839 until independence in 1967. By 1920 it was a major commercial centre of the Arabian Peninsula and supplied coal and salt to passing ships. The oil refinery began operating in 1954, and British Petroleum ran it and the port until the South Yemeni government took them over in 1978. Aden was the capital of South Yemen from 1967 until the union with North Yemen in 1990.

Aden is the principal city of Aden Governorate, which has eight districts. Its airport and the main offices of Aden University are at Khormaksar, on the isthmus that links the peninsulas to the mainland.
adolf-hitler: Adolf Hitler was born on 20 April 1889 in Braunau am Inn, a town in Austria-Hungary close to the border with Germany. He was the fourth of six children of Alois Hitler and his third wife, Klara Pölzl, and three siblings died in infancy. Alois was the illegitimate child of Maria Schicklgruber and bore her surname until 1876, when he took the name Hitler. Adolf's refusal to accept school discipline led to conflict with his father, who beat him; his mother tried to protect him. He moved to Germany in 1913.

In July 1919 Hitler was sent by the army to infiltrate the German Workers' Party (DAP), which he joined as member 555, the party having begun its count at 500 to seem larger. The party became the Nazi Party, and in 1921 he was appointed its leader. A coup attempt at Munich in 1923 failed; he was sentenced to five years in prison, served just over a year, and dictated the first volume of Mein Kampf there.

The Great Depression gave the party its opening: it won 107 seats in 1930, and after the elections of November 1932 it held the most seats in the Reichstag without a majority. Franz von Papen and other conservatives persuaded President Paul von Hindenburg to appoint Hitler chancellor on 30 January 1933. The Enabling Act of 23 March began the change to Nazi Germany, and after Hindenburg died on 2 August 1934 Hitler became head of state. Unemployment fell from six million in 1932 to fewer than one million in 1936. He ruled by the Führerprinzip, giving contradictory orders to set subordinates against one another.

Germany invaded Poland on 1 September 1939, and Hitler ordered the invasion of the Soviet Union in June 1941. By January 1942 he had decided that the Jews, Slavs and other deportees considered undesirable should be killed.

On 29 April 1945 Hitler married Eva Braun in the Führerbunker in Berlin, and the next day they killed themselves to avoid capture by the Soviet Red Army. Few Germans mourned him. The historian Ian Kershaw calls him the embodiment of modern political evil.

According to R. J. Rummel, the Nazi regime was responsible for the killing of an estimated 19.3 million civilians and prisoners of war, in addition to about six million Jews murdered in the Holocaust. A further 28.7 million soldiers and civilians died from military action in the European theatre. Germany suffered wholesale destruction, described as Stunde Null, or Zero Hour.
advance-australia-fair: Peter Dodds McCormick (1833–1916), a Scottish-born Australian composer, published the song in early December 1878 under the pen-name Amicus. It was first sung by Andrew Fairfax, with a concert band conducted by McCormick, at a function of the Highland Society of New South Wales in Sydney on 30 November 1878, Saint Andrew's Day. In a letter of 1 August 1913, McCormick said he had attended a concert at Sydney's Exhibition Building where various national anthems were played and felt aggravated that there was not one note for Australia. He wrote the first verse on the bus home and set it to music, and said the words and music came with ease.

The song grew in popularity, and an amended version was sung by a choir of around 10,000 at the inauguration of the Commonwealth of Australia on 1 January 1901. In 1907 the Australian Government awarded McCormick £100. The Australian Broadcasting Commission used it to announce its radio news bulletins from 1942 to 1952.

The original song had four verses. The second edition of 1879 begins Australia's sons let us rejoice, For we are young and free, and its second verse told of Cook raising Old England's flag, while its later verses spoke of Britannia and of rousing to arms against a foreign foe.

For the 1984 adoption the text was cut to two verses. The first was kept largely as the original, with the first line changed to Australians all let us rejoice, and the second is a modified form of the third verse sung at Federation in 1901, which begins Beneath our radiant Southern Cross. On 1 January 2021 the word young in the second line was replaced by one, in recognition of the legacy of Indigenous Australians.

The Whitlam government replaced God Save the Queen with Advance Australia Fair as the official national anthem in 1974, after an indicative opinion survey. The Fraser government restored God Save the Queen in January 1976 alongside three national songs: Advance Australia Fair, Waltzing Matilda and Song of Australia. A plebiscite in 1977 to choose the national song preferred Advance Australia Fair, and the Hawke government proclaimed it the national anthem in 1984. God Save the Queen became the royal anthem.

The song has drawn criticism for its archaic word girt and for a melody some call dull. It has also been criticised for failing to acknowledge Indigenous peoples; the line for we are young and free was said to ignore their long history. Versions in the Dharug language have been written, by Jacqueline Troy in 2003 and by Richard Green, performed in 2010. The version most often performed at official functions is a 1986 arrangement by Thomas Tycho.
aeneas: In Greek and Roman mythology Aeneas was the son of the Trojan prince Anchises and the goddess Aphrodite, known to the Romans as Venus. Anchises was a first cousin of King Priam of Troy, which made Aeneas a second cousin to Priam's children, among them Hector and Paris. The Homeric Hymn to Aphrodite tells how Zeus put desire for the mortal Anchises into Aphrodite, who bore Aeneas near Mount Ida and gave him to the nymphs of the mountain to raise.

In Homer's Iliad Aeneas is a minor character, the leader of the Trojans' Dardanian allies and a principal lieutenant of Hector. The gods twice save him from death, as if for a destiny not yet known. Aphrodite and Apollo rescue him from Diomedes, and Poseidon saves him from Achilles, noting that though from a junior branch of the royal family, he is destined to become king of the Trojan people.

Virgil's Aeneid tells the Roman form of the story. Aeneas is one of the few Trojans not killed or enslaved when Troy fell. Commanded by the gods to flee, he gathered the group known as the Aeneads, among them his father and his son Ascanius, and carried the household gods of Troy to Italy. Anchises died at Drepanum in Sicily. A storm brought the fleet to Carthage, where Aeneas had an affair with its queen, Dido. Mercury was sent to remind him of his mission and he left in secret. Dido cursed him, a curse said to set Carthage against Rome in the Punic Wars, and killed herself.

In Latium King Latinus welcomed the exiles. Turnus, king of the Rutuli, to whom Latinus's daughter Lavinia had been promised, made war on Aeneas at the urging of Juno and was killed, and there Virgil's account ends. According to Livy, Aeneas founded the city of Lavinium, named after his wife, and after his death Venus asked Jupiter to make him immortal, and he was recognised as the god Jupiter Indiges.

His son Ascanius, also called Iulus, founded Alba Longa. In the Aeneid, Romulus and Remus descend from Aeneas through their mother Rhea Silvia, and the Julian family of Rome, among them Julius Cæsar and Augustus, traced its lineage to him and so to Venus.
afghanistan: Afghanistan is a landlocked country at the crossroads of Central and South Asia, occupying 652,864 square kilometres. It is predominantly mountainous, dominated by the Hindu Kush range, which ends in the west-central highlands and separates the plains of the north, the Turkestan Plains, from those of the southwest, the Sistan Basin. The highest point is Noshaq, at 7,492 metres. Its longest border, the Durand Line, is with Pakistan.

People lived in what is now Afghanistan at least 50,000 years ago, and farming communities there were among the earliest in the world. Urban civilisation is believed to have begun as early as 3000 BCE, and Mundigak, near Kandahar, was a centre of the Helmand culture; an Indus Valley site has been found at Shortugai on the Oxus River. After 2000 BCE successive waves of semi-nomadic people from Central Asia, among them many Indo-Iranians, moved south.

By the middle of the 6th century BCE the Achaemenids had overthrown the Medes and incorporated Arachosia, Aria and Bactria, and the tombstone inscription of Darius the Great lists the Kabul Valley among the 29 countries he conquered. Because of its conquests and periods in both the Iranian and Indian cultural spheres, the area was a centre for Zoroastrianism, Buddhism, Hinduism and later Islam.

The modern state began with the Durrani Empire in the 18th century under Ahmad Shah Durrani, although Dost Mohammad Khan is sometimes considered the founder of the first modern Afghan state. The name Afghanistan became a state designation only during the colonial interventions of the 19th century. Afghanistan was a buffer state in the Great Game between the British and Russian empires. The British were repelled in the First Anglo-Afghan War, but won the Second. After the Third Anglo-Afghan War in 1919 the country became free of foreign political hegemony, and the independent Kingdom of Afghanistan emerged in 1926.

Since the late 1970s warfare has dominated Afghanistan's history. In 1973 King Zahir Shah was overthrown by his cousin Mohammad Daoud Khan, and a communist revolution in 1978 killed Daoud Khan. The Soviet Union invaded in 1979 and withdrew in 1989 after the mujahideen won the Soviet–Afghan War, and a civil war followed. The Taliban controlled most of the country by 1996, were overthrown in the 2001 United States invasion, and returned to power in 2021. The population is estimated at between 35 and 50 million, and about 70.4% live in rural areas.
africa: Africa covers about 30.3 million square kilometres, including adjacent islands, around 20% of Earth's land area. It straddles the equator and the prime meridian and is joined to Asia by the Isthmus of Suez, 163 kilometres wide. Its coastline is 26,000 kilometres long, and the absence of deep indentations means that Europe, a third of its size, has a longer one. The climate ranges from tropical to subarctic on the highest peaks: the northern half is primarily desert or arid, the centre and south hold savanna plains and rainforest, and 60% of the land surface consists of drylands and deserts. Algeria is the largest country by area.

Africa is widely accepted as the place of origin of humans. The earliest hominids and their ancestors have been dated to around 7 million years ago, and Homo sapiens is believed to have originated there 350,000 to 260,000 years ago, before the Out of Africa II migration of about 50,000 years ago.

African societies have generally recorded their history through oral tradition, which anthropologists have termed oral civilisations. The continent saw the rise and fall of many kingdoms and empires, among them Ancient Egypt, Makuria, the Fatimids, Mali, the Asante, Kongo, the Luba, Great Zimbabwe and the Zulu, although many societies were heterarchical and stateless. Slave trades created diasporas, especially in the Americas.

From the late 19th century to the early 20th century most of Africa was conquered and colonised by European nations, except Ethiopia and Liberia. Colonies were maintained for the economic exploitation and extraction of natural resources. Most present states emerged from decolonisation after the Second World War, and in 1963 they established the Organisation of African Unity, the predecessor of the African Union. The new countries decided to keep their colonial borders, using traditional power structures in governance to varying degrees.

The continent has 54 fully recognised sovereign states, and the African Union, which succeeded the Organisation of African Unity in 2001, has 55 member states and is headquartered in Addis Ababa. Africa's population was estimated at 1,394 million in 2021, up from 229 million in 1950, and it is the youngest among the continents. Bantu-speaking peoples are the majority in southern, central and southeast Africa.
african-national-congress: The African National Congress was founded in Bloemfontein on 8 January 1912 as the South African Native National Congress, and took its present name in 1923. It was a successor of the Cape Colony's Imbumba Yamanyama organisation. Its founders were Pixley ka Isaka Seme, Sol Plaatje, John Langalibalele Dube and Walter Rubusana, who, like much of the early membership, came from the conservative, educated and religious professional classes of black South African society. Xhosa chiefs did not take part but showed great support, and King Jongilizwe donated 50 cows at the founding. Around 1920 the organisation moved partly away from the politics of petitioning towards a programme of passive resistance aimed chiefly at the pass laws.

In the 1940s Alfred Bitini Xuma revived some of Gumede's programmes, and in 1944 a left-wing Youth League formed under Walter Sisulu, Nelson Mandela and Oliver Tambo. After the National Party came to power in 1948 on a platform of apartheid, the new generation pushed through a Programme of Action advocating African nationalism and the sustained use of strikes, stay-aways and boycotts. This culminated in the Defiance Campaign of 1952–53, organised with the Indian Congress and the coloured Franchise Action Council. In June 1955 the Congress of the People at Kliptown ratified the Freedom Charter, which became a fundamental document of the struggle.

The Charter was used as a pretext to prosecute hundreds of activists in the Treason Trial. After the Sharpeville massacre on 21 March 1960 the government banned the ANC, and it remained banned until February 1990. Increasing state repression forced it into exile. Headquartered in Lusaka, Zambia, it pursued sabotage and guerrilla warfare through its military wing, uMkhonto weSizwe, founded in 1961 with the South African Communist Party. It became a key player in the negotiations to end apartheid that began after the ban was lifted. The first post-apartheid election in 1994 resulted in Nelson Mandela being elected President of South Africa.

Every member belongs to a local branch, and branch members choose policies and leaders mainly by electing delegates to the National Conference, held every five years. Between conferences an 86-member National Executive Committee leads the organisation. It has three autonomous leagues, for women, youth and veterans, and leads the Tripartite Alliance with the South African Communist Party and the Congress of South African Trade Unions, formalised in mid-1990. Its flag has black, green and gold stripes.
agamemnon: In Greek mythology Agamemnon was a descendant of Pelops, son of Tantalus. According to the common story, told in Homer's Iliad and Odyssey, he and his younger brother Menelaus were the sons of Atreus, king of Mycenae, and Aerope, daughter of the Cretan king Catreus. His father Atreus murdered the sons of his twin brother Thyestes and fed them to him. Thyestes' son Aegisthus then killed Atreus and took the throne of Mycenae. Agamemnon and Menelaus took refuge with Tyndareus, King of Sparta, who brought them back to Mycenae, where they drove out Thyestes.

In Sparta, Agamemnon and Menelaus married Tyndareus' daughters Clytemnestra and Helen. Menelaus succeeded Tyndareus as king of Sparta, while Agamemnon, with his brother's help, drove out Aegisthus and Thyestes to recover his father's kingdom, and he extended his dominion by conquest to become the most powerful prince in Greece. In Aeschylus' Oresteia he has a son, Orestes, and two daughters, Iphigenia and Electra.

Agamemnon gathered the Greek forces to sail for Troy. At Aulis, in Boeotia, the army incurred the anger of the goddess Artemis, and plague and a lack of wind stopped the fleet. The prophet Calchas announced that the goddess could be appeased only by the sacrifice of Agamemnon's daughter Iphigenia, and the classical dramatists differ on how willing father and daughter were.

The Iliad tells of his quarrel with Achilles in the final year of the war. Agamemnon took Chryseis as a war prize and, when Apollo sent a plague, reluctantly returned her, then seized Achilles' prize Briseis in compensation. Achilles withdrew from the fighting. Agamemnon later sent ambassadors to Achilles with offers of riches and his daughter's hand, which Achilles refused until his companion Patroclus was killed by Hector. They were reconciled in Book Nineteen. He is described as a representative of kingly authority, whose chief fault was haughtiness, and as one of the three best warriors on the Greek side.

After the fall of Troy, Cassandra, the daughter of Priam, fell to Agamemnon as a prize. On his return he was killed. In the oldest versions he was slain by Aegisthus, and in Homer's Odyssey Aegisthus ambushes him at a feast. In Pindar and the tragedians he is killed in a bath by Clytemnestra, as in Aeschylus' Oresteia. Orestes later avenged him by killing Aegisthus and his own mother, and was pursued by the Erinyes until he was absolved. In Sparta he was worshipped as Zeus Agamemnon, and his tomb was pointed out among the ruins of Mycenae and at Amyclae.
agartala: Agartala lies in the plain of Tripura on the banks of the Haora (also written Saidra) River, about 2 kilometres east of the border with Bangladesh and about 2,499 km from New Delhi. The river flows through the city and floods each year in the monsoon. The climate is humid subtropical, with long, hot and wet summers from April to October and a short, mild winter from mid-November to early March. The name combines agar, the perfume and incense tree of the genus Aquilaria, with tala, 'underneath', a reference to the density of agarwood trees in the region.

Tripura served as the capital of several Hindu kingdoms. No timeline of rulers has been found, but records name as many as 179 Hindu rulers, from the mythological King Druhya to Kirit Bikram Kishore Manikya, the last king. Tripura also came under Mughal rule, and under British governance in 1808. The older capital of the princely state, then called Swadhin Tripura, was at Rangamati on the Gomati River, in what is now Udaipur. Its move to the present Old Agartala, called Haveli, is dated to 1760 and credited to the Manikya rulers.

The founding of the capital city of Agartala is dated to 1838, under Maharaja Krishna Kishore Manikya, and the shift from Old Haveli to New Haveli, the present Agartala, to 1849. The reasons given are frequent invasions by the Kukis and the wish for easy communication with British Bengal. The Ujjayanta Palace, the palace of the Tripura kings, was named by the poet Rabindranath Tagore, who visited Tripura many times. It served as the meeting place of the Tripura Legislative Assembly until 2011 and is now a museum. In 1941 the city had 17,693 inhabitants.

Agartala is the capital and largest city of the Indian state of Tripura, and it is governed by the Agartala Municipal Corporation, which was formed on 21 January 2014. Bengali is the dominant language, with Kokborok also spoken, and the population is mainly Bengali and Tripuri. The Bengali influence reflects royal patronage and the arrival of Bengalis from Comilla, Sylhet, Noakhali and Chittagong. Hinduism is the main religion and Christianity widespread. Durga Puja and Saraswati Puja are major festivals, and the Tripuri festivals Kharchi and Garia are also known. Its 2011 census population was 400,004.
age-of-discovery: The Age of Discovery is dated c. 1418 to c. 1620. Its background lay in trade. For centuries the Republic of Venice and neighbouring maritime republics held the monopoly of European trade with the Middle East, and the silk and spice trade made them very rich. Muslim traders dominated the Indian Ocean routes, with Calicut a main emporium, and the overland routes into Asia were blocked by wars and banditry as the Mongol states disintegrated. The Crusades, though not a military success, had brought Europe into contact with the Middle East and its goods.

The Portuguese began systematically exploring the Atlantic coast of Africa in 1418 under the sponsorship of Prince Henry the Navigator, and in 1488 Bartolomeu Dias reached the Indian Ocean by that route. Portugal had rejected Christopher Columbus's plan to reach India by sailing west in 1485 and 1488, its experts judging his estimate of the distance too low.

In 1492 the Catholic Monarchs of Spain funded Columbus's Atlantic crossing, and he reached a continent unmapped by Europeans, though the Norse had explored it 500 years earlier. The Treaty of Tordesillas, ratified by Pope Julius II, divided the zones of exploration between Portugal and Castile. In 1498 Vasco da Gama established a sea route to India. Vasco Núñez de Balboa became the first European to see the Pacific from the New World on 25 September 1513, and the Magellan expedition of 1519–1522 under Juan Sebastián Elcano completed the first circumnavigation.

Spain's conquistadors, who were more like soldiers of fortune than an army, conquered Mexico (1519–1521) and Peru (1532–1533) and formed alliances with some indigenous peoples. In 1565 Andrés de Urdaneta found the return route across the Pacific, reaching Acapulco on 8 October 1565 after 130 days, and the Manila galleon trade linked the Americas and Asia until 1815. France, the Netherlands and England did not recognise the Treaty of Tordesillas and challenged Iberian power. Russia, meanwhile, moved into Siberia.

Contact between the Old and New Worlds produced the Columbian exchange of plants, animals, people, including slaves, diseases and culture. Cattle, horses and sheep went west, and tobacco, potatoes, tomatoes and maize came east. The era began the global silver trade between the Americas, Europe and China. It also brought the enslavement, exploitation and conquest of Indigenous peoples, and European diseases such as smallpox decimated indigenous populations.

The term itself has been scrutinised. J. H. Parry called the period the Age of Reconnaissance and stressed its expansion of geographical knowledge and empirical science, while Edmundo O'Gorman, as Anthony Pagden reports, argued that Europeans' effort to fit the new knowledge into their worldview mattered more than the encounter, in what he called the invention of America.
aguascalientes: Aguascalientes lies in the northern part of the Bajío region in north-central Mexico, about 480 km from Mexico City, at an average altitude of 1,950 m. It is bordered by Zacatecas to the north, east and west and by Jalisco to the south, and covers 5,471 km2. Its climate is predominantly semi-arid, with a temperate highland climate in the Sierra Fría range. The name means hot waters and comes from the abundance of hot springs found in the area.

Arrowheads and rock paintings show that people lived here for more than 20,000 years. Before the Spanish arrived the land was inhabited by Chichimecas, specifically the Guachichil. To protect the Camino de la Plata, the silver road between Zacatecas and Mexico City, the Spanish built presidios. The king ordered the judge Gerónimo de Orozco to find a rich man to settle the territory and expel the Chichimecas, and Juan de Montoro founded the town of Aguas Calientes on 22 October 1575.

In 1789 the sub-delegation of Aguascalientes became a dependency of Zacatecas. A decree of Santa Anna dated 23 May 1835 ordered its separation but was never made official, and Aguascalientes continued to belong to Zacatecas. It was included as a state in the draft constitution of 1856, passed by the 79 deputies present, which established the state on 10 December 1856.

The state has 11 municipalities, and most of its people live in the metropolitan area of its capital, also called Aguascalientes. It was once a major silver miner and a centre of railroad transport, thanks to its position between Mexico City, Guadalajara and Monterrey. Its San Marcos Fair is regarded as the national fair of Mexico.
ahvaz: Ahvaz stands on the banks of the Karun River in the Khuzestan plain, at an elevation of 12 m, near the border with Iraq. The Karun is the largest river in Iran by volume and flows through the centre of the city, which is known for the many large bridges that join its east and west parts. The older, residential part of the city lies on the left bank, the newer administrative and industrial district on the right. The climate is hot desert, with long, hot summers.

A settlement here is traced to the Achaemenid period under the name Taryana, on the Royal Road from Persepolis to Sardis. Under Ardashir I it was refounded on both sides of the river as Hormazd-Ardeshir, later shortened to Darawashir, and became capital of the province of Susiana. After the Muslim defeat of the Sasanian Empire in the 7th century CE, the western part, Horamshir, was destroyed and the Arabs rendered the market quarter's name as Sūq al-Ahvāz. The name Ahvaz is the Arabicized plural of Huzi, the old people of the region, from whom Khuzestan also takes its name.

In the 19th century Ahvaz was a small borough: 1,500 to 2,000 inhabitants according to Ainsworth in 1835, and 700 according to Curzon in 1890. In the 1880s the Karun was dredged and reopened to commerce, and a port, Bandar-e-Naseri, named for Naser al-Din Shah Qajar, grew beside the old village. Oil was found nearby in the early 20th century. The provincial government moved there from Shushtar in 1926, and the Trans-Iranian Railway reached the city in 1929. Iraq tried to annex Khuzestan in 1980, starting the Iran–Iraq War (1980–1988), and Ahvaz, close to the front lines, suffered severely.

Ahvaz is the capital of Khuzestan province, with more than 1.3 million people in its metropolitan area. Persian is the official language; Khuzestani Arabic, Bakhtiari and other languages are also spoken, and Neo-Mandaic is used among the Mandaeans. The city has been called the City of Bridges and the Oil Capital of Iran. Shahid Chamran University of Ahvaz, founded in 1955 as Gondishapur University, is the oldest institution of higher education in the city.
ain: Ain is made up of four areas: Bresse, Dombes, Bugey and the Pays de Gex. In the north the plain of Bresse is bordered by the river Saône. In the south-east the Dombes has more than a thousand ponds and lakes, and in the east the southern Jura Mountains overlook the Bresse plain. The Gex region, which belongs geographically to the Lake Geneva basin, is separated from the rest by the last eastern chain of the Jura. In the alphabetical ordering of French departments Ain comes first and so has the number 01.

The first inhabitants settled about 15000 BCE, and the Calendar of Coligny, of the late 2nd century BCE, bears the oldest surviving Gaulish inscription. In 58 BCE Julius Caesar's action against the Helvetians, advancing over this territory, began the Gallic Wars. In the 6th century the diocese of Belley became the first bishopric in the region. The first large lordships emerged between 895 and 900 at Bâgé-le-Châtel, the nucleus of Bresse, and at Coligny.

In 1272 Sibylle de Bâgé married Amadeus V, Count of Savoy, and added Bresse to Savoy's domains. By the start of the 15th century almost the whole region was united under the house of Savoy. The Treaty of Lyon of 17 January 1601 ended the Franco-Savoyard War and Ain now belonged to Burgundy. The department was created in 1790, during the French Revolution.

The prefecture of Ain is Bourg-en-Bresse. The department lies on the Swiss border, adjoining the cantons of Geneva and Vaud. Its agriculture includes the poultry of Bresse, the carp of the Dombes and the wine of Bugey, and most of CERN's Large Hadron Collider lies in communes of the Arrondissement of Gex.
aircraft-carrier: The aircraft carrier followed the first flight of the Wright brothers at Kitty Hawk in 1903. On 14 November 1910 Eugene Burton Ely made the first experimental take-off of a Curtiss Pusher airplane from a United States Navy ship, the cruiser USS Birmingham. On 9 May 1912 Commander Charles Samson of the Royal Naval Air Service made the first take-off from a ship under way, flying from the battleship HMS Hibernia, the first practical demonstration of the carrier at sea.

Early in the First World War the Japanese ship Wakamiya conducted the first carrier-launched air raid, on 6 September 1914, lowering Farman seaplanes into the water by crane to attack ships off Qingdao. Neither target was hit. The first airstrike by aircraft flown off a carrier was the Tondern raid in July 1918, when seven Sopwith Camels launched from HMS Furious damaged a German airbase and destroyed two zeppelins.

An aircraft carrier is a warship with a full-length flight deck and hangar that make it a mobile airbase at sea. It lets a naval force project air power far from national territory without relying on local airfields. Since the Second World War the carrier has replaced the battleship as the flagship of a fleet, and it has largely changed naval battle from gunfire to air strikes beyond visual range.

Fleet carriers operate with the main fleet and are the largest and fastest. Escort carriers, smaller and slower, defended convoys and were often built on merchant hulls. Light carriers were fast enough for the main fleet but smaller. Aircraft are launched by catapult (CATOBAR), which suits heavy jets, or by short take-off and vertical landing (STOVL), which is cheaper to operate.

Only about 20 aircraft can be on the flight deck at once, and most are kept in a hangar several decks below and raised by elevator. Munitions are stored low, usually below the waterline so the area can be flooded in an emergency.

Carriers have been called the largest weapon system ever created. Admiral Sir Mark Stanhope of the Royal Navy said that countries that aspire to strategic international influence have aircraft carriers, and Henry Kissinger called one 100,000 tons of diplomacy. A few have been kept as museum ships, among them USS Yorktown, USS Intrepid and USS Midway.
aisha: Aisha was born in Mecca c. 614, the daughter of Abu Bakr and Umm Ruman, two of Muhammad's companions. The sources give little more about her childhood. After the death of Muhammad's first wife, Khadija bint Khuwaylid, his aunt Khawlah bint Hakim proposed that he marry Aisha, and her earlier engagement to Jubayr ibn Mut'im was annulled. The orientalist W. Montgomery Watt suggests that Muhammad hoped to strengthen his ties with Abu Bakr, as marriages in Arabian culture commonly did.

All extant hadiths agree that the marriage took place in Mecca but was not consummated until the month of Shawwal after the hijrah to Medina, in April 623. Classical sources give her age as six at marriage and nine at consummation, though Ibn Hisham's biography suggests she may have been ten. Her age later became a subject of modern debate.

In Sunni tradition Aisha ranks second only to Khadija among Muhammad's wives in his affection. Muhammad died in her apartment in Medina. She remained active in the Muslim community for 44 years afterwards and is credited with narrating over 2,000 hadiths, on ritual, inheritance, pilgrimage and other subjects. She issued legal opinions, and companions such as Urwah ibn al-Zubayr consulted her. She was known by the title al-Ṣiddīqa bint al-Ṣiddīq, "the truthful woman, daughter of the truthful man".

In 656 the third caliph, Uthman, was killed by rebels, which began the First Fitna. Aisha, with Talha ibn Ubayd Allah and al-Zubayr ibn al-Awwam, mobilised forces against the new caliph, Ali, demanding punishment for those responsible. The two sides met near Basra in the Battle of the Camel, named after the camel on which Aisha directed her troops from a howdah. Her forces were defeated and about 10,000 Muslims were killed, in what is considered the first major battle between Muslims.

Ali reproached Aisha but pardoned her and sent her back to Medina under an escort led by her brother, Muhammad ibn Abi Bakr. She withdrew from public politics and became a teacher, and in her last two years she spent much time telling stories of Muhammad. She died at her home in Medina on 17 Ramadan 58 AH (16 July 678). Abu Hurayra led her funeral prayer, and she was buried in the al-Baqi cemetery.
Sunni Islam reveres her as a leading scholar, hadith transmitter and teacher of several companions and of the tabi'in. Shia Muslims generally view her critically because of her opposition to Ali.
aix-en-provence: Aix-en-Provence lies in the south of France, about 30 km north of Marseille, in a plain overlooking the Arc river. The Montagne Sainte-Victoire can be seen to the east. The city has a Mediterranean climate, warm and sunny, though more extreme than Marseille's because of its inland position, and it is partly sheltered from the Mistral. Its old town, with narrow streets and mansions of the 16th, 17th and 18th centuries, lies north of the Cours Mirabeau, a wide avenue that follows the line of the old city wall.

The city was founded in 123 BCE by the Roman consul Sextius Calvinus, who gave his name to its springs, after the nearby Gallic oppidum at Entremont had been destroyed. In 102 BCE the Romans under Gaius Marius defeated the Ambrones and Teutones in its vicinity. In the 4th century CE Aix became the metropolis of Narbonensis Secunda. The Visigoths occupied it in 477, the Franks and Lombards plundered it repeatedly in the following century, and it was occupied by the Saracens in 731 and by Charles Martel in 737.

In the Middle Ages Aix was the capital of Provence and reached its height after the 12th century, when under the houses of Barcelona and Aragon and then Anjou it became an artistic centre and seat of learning. Louis II of Anjou granted a royal charter for a university in 1409. Provence passed to the French crown in 1487, and in 1501 Louis XII established the parliament of Provence in Aix, which lasted until 1789. In the 17th and 18th centuries the town was the seat of the Intendance of Provence.

Aix-en-Provence is a subprefecture of the department of Bouches-du-Rhône, with about 148,000 inhabitants, and remains a university town. Its Cathedral of the Holy Saviour stands on the site of a Roman forum and combines styles from the 5th to the 17th century, with a Merovingian baptistery and a Romanesque cloister. The Festival d'Aix-en-Provence, an opera festival, was founded in 1948. The painter Paul Cézanne was born in the city, as was the composer Darius Milhaud. The older streets still carry names in both Provençal and French.
ajmer: Ajmer lies in a valley of the Aravalli Range in the Indian state of Rajasthan, on the lower slopes of Taragarh Hill. Its name comes from Ajaya Meru, Sanskrit for invincible hill, given by a Chahamana ruler, either Ajayaraja I or Ajayaraja II, and referring to Taragarh Hill. To the northwest the Nagapathar Range protects it from the spread of the Thar Desert. Because of its central position in the state it is called the Heart of Rajasthan.

The sources disagree on the founding. A prashasti issued by Vigraharaja IV states that Ajayadeva, meaning Ajayaraja II, moved his residence to Ajmer, and the earliest mention of the city's name is in a text copied in 1113 CE, so Ajmer existed before then. A later text says the 8th-century king Ajayaraja I built the fort that became Taragarh, and a historian, R. B. Singh, finds this likely since inscriptions of the 8th century have been found there. Singh suggests that Ajayaraja II expanded the town, built palaces and moved the Chahamana capital there from Shakambhari. In 1193 the Ghurids annexed Ajmer, and it was later returned to Gaur Rajput rulers on condition of tribute. By the 15th century Mewar had captured it.

Akbar conquered Ajmer in 1556 and made it capital of the Ajmer Subah. The Mughals made frequent pilgrimages to the dargah of Moinuddin Chishti, and Jahanara Begum and Dara Shikoh, children of Shah Jahan, were born there in 1614 and 1615. Mughal patronage waned by the early 18th century. The Scindias conquered the city in 1752, and the British gained authority in 1818. Under British rule it was headquarters of the Ajmer-Merwara Province, and Mayo College was founded in 1875 for the sons of chiefs and nobles. After independence in 1947 Ajmer continued as a separate state until 1956, when it was merged into Rajasthan.

Ajmer is the administrative headquarters of its district and division, and had 542,321 inhabitants in the 2011 census. The Ajmer Sharif Dargah, the shrine of Khwaja Moinuddin Chishti at the foot of Taragarh Hill, has white marble buildings around two courtyards and draws many pilgrims. Other sights include Taragarh Fort, the mosque known as Adhai Din Ka Jhonpra, Akbar's fort, now a museum, and the Ana Sagar Lake. The temple town of Pushkar lies a few kilometres away.
akhenaten: Akhenaten was born Amenhotep IV, a younger son of the pharaoh Amenhotep III and his principal wife, Tiye. His elder brother, the crown prince Thutmose, was recognised as heir, but Thutmose's early death, perhaps around the 30th regnal year of Amenhotep III, left Amenhotep IV next in line. Little is known of his youth. Donald Redford dates his birth to c. 1363–1361 BCE, and the only certain servant of the prince is Parennefer, whose tomb mentions him.

He married Nefertiti, his Great Royal Wife, at a date that is not known. A secondary wife, Kiya, is also attested. He had seven attested daughters, six of them by Nefertiti, among them Meritaten and Ankhesenamun. Tutankhamun was his son-in-law and is considered likely to have been his son as well.

Amenhotep IV took the throne most likely in 1353 or 1351 BCE, at an age estimated anywhere from 10 to 23. Scholars disagree whether he shared power with his father for up to 12 years or not at all. Eric Cline, Nicholas Reeves and Peter Dorman argue for no coregency or one of at most two years, while Donald Redford and others reject any. In the fifth year of his reign he changed his name to Akhenaten, meaning 'Effective for the Aten'.

Worship of the sun had grown under the Eighteenth Dynasty, and Amenhotep III had given the Aten royal patronage, but he still devoted himself chiefly to Amun-Ra. Redford traced three stages in Atenism. In the first the disc still rested on the head of the falcon-headed Ra-Horakhty. In the second the Aten was raised above other gods and its name was placed in cartouches. In the last it was shown as a disc whose rays end in human hands. Egyptologists differ on whether the religion was monotheistic, monolatristic or henotheistic.

Amarna art, which flourished under Akhenaten and his immediate successors, is more naturalistic and shows more movement than traditional Egyptian art. Akhenaten himself is drawn with a sagging stomach, broad hips, thin legs and a long face. Some have argued that this reflects a medical condition, but Dominic Montserrat reports a broad consensus among Egyptologists that the forms are not to be read literally, and suggests they made the king a symbol of the androgyny of the Aten.

After his death his monuments were dismantled and hidden, his statues destroyed and his name left out of later lists of rulers, and traditional worship was gradually restored, notably under Tutankhamun. Later rulers called him 'the enemy' or 'that criminal'. He was almost lost to history until the late 19th-century discovery of Amarna, the city he built. A mummy found in tomb KV55 in 1907 may be his, although its identification has been questioned.
akim-oda: Akim Oda lies in the south of Ghana, surrounded by rain forest, in the basin of the Birim River, which flows through the town and is rich in gold and diamonds. The climate is semi-equatorial and wet. Rain falls heavily from April to June and again from September to November, and a dry season, with markedly lower temperatures, lasts from December to February. The town is the capital of the Birim Central Municipal District and had 60,604 residents as of 2013.

Cocoa is grown on formal and informal plantations, sometimes along the roads; the harvested beans are dried and kept in warehouses until they are shipped. North of the Birim there are palm oil plantations covering roughly 6,000 hectares, most of them small and independently owned, and bamboo is also cultivated. Local miners take gold and diamonds from the river bank by traditional methods, often with simple tools.

The forests near the town are cut for timber. Ghana's forest cover shrank from 8.2 million hectares in 1900 to 1.6 million in 2000, and forest plantations are being established near Akim Oda under the National Forest Plantation Development Program. Visitors are shown a tree described as the largest in West Africa, 12 metres in circumference and 66.5 metres high, and may see the mining from dug-out boats and ceremonies with Akan drumming.

The Akim Oda Government Hospital serves the Kotoku traditional area and takes referrals from nearby communities in the Akyem states; private hospitals in the town also serve Akyem Bosome and part of the Abuakwa traditional area. The public sector has more than fifteen primary and junior high schools and three senior high schools, and four radio stations broadcast from the town.
akita-prefecture: Akita Prefecture lies on the north-western side of Honshu, in the Tōhoku region, on the coast of the Sea of Japan. It borders Aomori Prefecture to the north, Iwate to the east, Miyagi to the southeast and Yamagata to the south. Its borders roughly form a rectangle 169 kilometres from north to south and 86 kilometres from west to east, covering 11,637 square kilometres. The Oga Peninsula is a prominent feature of the western edge, the Ōu Mountains, the longest range in Japan, mark the eastern border, and the higher Dewa Mountains run through the centre. Winters are cold, especially away from the sea.

The region was created from the ancient provinces of Dewa and Mutsu. Separated from the main centres of Japanese commerce, politics and population by several hundred kilometres and by mountain ranges, Akita remained largely isolated from Japanese society until after the year 600, and was a region of hunter-gatherers and principally nomadic tribes. The first historical record dates to 658, when Abe no Hirafu, governor of Koshi Province, conquered the native Ezo tribes at what are now the cities of Akita and Noshiro and built a fort on the Mogami River, which began Japanese settlement.

In 733 a new military settlement, later renamed Akita Castle, was built in what is now the Takashimizu area of Akita. The region served as a base from which the Japanese empire drove the Ezo people from northern Honshu. Under the Tokugawa shogunate it was given to the Satake clan, who ruled it for 260 years and developed the agriculture and mining that remain important. In 1871, during the Meiji Restoration, Dewa Province was reshaped and the old daimyō domains were abolished, which produced the modern borders of Akita.

The city of Akita is the capital and largest city, and Yokote, Daisen and Yurihonjō are other major cities. The economy has long rested on agriculture, fishing and forestry, and the prefecture is known for rice and sake. Population has declined since 1955. Kakunodate preserves many samurai houses, among them the former home of Odano Naotake, who illustrated Japan's first modern guide to human anatomy. The Namahage ritual in Oga on New Year's Eve and the Akita Kantō festival in August are among its best-known customs.
akkadian-empire: The Akkadian Empire takes its name from the city and region of Akkad, near the confluence of the Tigris and Euphrates. The city has not yet been identified on the ground, but it is known from textual sources, at least one of them older than Sargon's reign. The period is generally dated to 2334–2154 BCE by the middle chronology; the short-chronology dates of 2270–2083 BCE are now considered less likely. It followed the Early Dynastic Period and was succeeded by the Ur III Period, though both transitions are blurry.

Its founder, Sargon, was a usurper, and he is not known to have had a father or predecessor on the throne of Akkad, until then a marginal city. Later texts make it hard to separate legend from reality. Some historians, drawing on a late legend, suggest he rebelled against Ur-Zababa of Kish, but this is hypothetical. He then faced Lugal-zage-si of Uruk, the most powerful king in the south, and according to copies of his inscriptions defeated him around 2300 BCE. Lugal-zage-si was captured, made to wear a yoke and paraded at Nippur.

Sargon installed loyal governors in several Sumerian cities and so created a kingdom covering all of southern Mesopotamia, with Akkad as its capital. His influence is said to have stretched from the Mediterranean to Iran, and expeditions went as far as Dilmun and Magan. His sons Rimush and Manishtushu struggled to keep control, and both may have died violently. Sargon's grandson Naram-Sin called himself King of the Four Quarters and had himself called god of Akkad, with a cult in his honour, though whether he was considered a full deity is debated.

Naram-Sin's successors were weaker. The empire collapsed, probably through a combination of internal unrest, severe environmental and economic stress from a drought associated with the 4.2-kiloyear climate event, and threats from the Gutians, Amorites and Elamites.

The Akkadian language became the empire's lingua franca, while Sumerian stayed important in religion and literature. The kings had their exploits written in long inscriptions on stelae and statues, and their royal art, with a more naturalistic sculpture centred on the king, had a lasting influence on Mesopotamian art. Enheduanna, Sargon's daughter, served as high priestess and is often recognised as the first known named author in history. The kingdom of the Third Dynasty of Ur stood in the tradition of the first empire. Later, Sargon became the example to follow and Naram-Sin the example to avoid, and several rulers took the title King of Akkad.
akkadian-language: Akkadian is an East Semitic language attested in ancient Mesopotamia from the mid-third millennium BCE. It is the earliest documented Semitic language and is named after the city of Akkad, a major centre during the Akkadian Empire (c. 2334–2154 BCE). Akkadian names appear in Sumerian texts from the mid-3rd millennium BCE, and texts fully in Akkadian begin to appear from about the 24th century BCE.

It was written in cuneiform, adopted from the Sumerians. Sargon of Akkad's empire introduced Akkadian as a written language by adapting Sumerian cuneiform. In the Middle Bronze Age it virtually displaced Sumerian, assumed to have been extinct as a living language by the 18th century BCE. By the 20th century BCE two forms were in use, Assyrian and Babylonian.

Akkadian is a fusional language with grammatical case, and like other Semitic languages it builds words on consonantal roots, most of them of three consonants. It has three cases and three numbers, though the dual is vestigial. Unlike most Semitic languages it uses subject–object–verb word order. Sumerian influenced its phonology, vocabulary and syntax, and scholars describe the two languages as a sprachbund.

Cuneiform suited it poorly, since it could not represent the glottal stop, the pharyngeals and the emphatic consonants. Scribes used signs as Sumerian logograms, Sumerian syllables or Akkadian syllables. The sign AN, for example, can stand for ilum ('god'), for the god Anu or for the syllable -an-.

In its Assyrian and Babylonian forms Akkadian was the native language of the Mesopotamian empires through the later Bronze Age and became the lingua franca of much of the Ancient Near East by the time of the Bronze Age collapse c. 1150 BCE. It declined under the Neo-Assyrian Empire, by about the 8th century BCE, in favour of Old Aramaic. By the Hellenistic period only scholars and priests in the temples used it, and the last known Akkadian cuneiform document dates from the 1st century CE.

Hundreds of thousands of texts and fragments survive, including religious narrative, legal and scientific works and letters. Literary works include the Atrahasis Epic, the Enûma Elish, the Amarna letters and the Epic of Gilgamesh. The Chicago Assyrian Dictionary, in 21 volumes, was begun in 1921 and completed in 2011.
al-andalus: Al-Andalus refers to the territories of the Iberian Peninsula under Muslim rule between 711 and 1492, a name first attested on dinars minted in 716 with inscriptions in Latin and Arabic. At its widest extent under Umayyad rule it covered most of the peninsula and Septimania in southern France. It was first divided into five administrative units, corresponding roughly to Andalusia, Castile and León, Navarre, Aragon and Catalonia, Portugal and Galicia, and Languedoc-Roussillon. Its boundaries then shrank in a series of conquests that Western historiography has traditionally called the Reconquista, until only the Emirate of Granada remained.

In 711 Tariq ibn-Ziyad led an army of 7,000 that landed at Gibraltar on 30 April, ostensibly to intervene in a Visigothic civil war. After a victory over King Roderic at the Battle of Guadalete on 19 July 711, he and Musa ibn Nusayr brought most of the Visigothic Kingdom under Muslim rule in seven years. Al-Andalus was first a province of the Umayyad Caliphate, with Córdoba as its capital. It became the Emirate of Córdoba (c. 750–929) and then the Caliphate of Córdoba (929–1031), under which Córdoba became a leading cultural and economic centre. Resistant Visigoths took refuge in the Cantabrian highlands and formed the Kingdom of Asturias.

After 1031 al-Andalus split into taifa states. The Christian capture of Toledo in 1085 brought in the Almoravid Empire, and then the Almohad Caliphate, both based in Marrakesh. In the 13th century most of the south fell to Portuguese, Castilian and Aragonese conquests. The Emirate of Granada (1238–1492), a tributary of the Crown of Castile, surrendered to the Catholic Monarchs in 1492.

Society in al-Andalus consisted of Muslims, Christians and Jews, with Arabs at the top, followed by Berbers, Muladies, Mozarabs and Jews. Non-Muslims had the status of ahl al-dhimma and paid a tax, and scholars still debate their treatment. Andalusi scholars advanced trigonometry (Jabir ibn Aflah), astronomy (al-Zarqali), surgery (al-Zahrawi), pharmacology (Ibn Zuhr) and agronomy. Alfonso X of Castile and other Christian monarchs had Andalusi libraries translated into Latin.

Many Muslims were forced to convert in the later Reconquista, particularly after the decrees of 1502 and 1526, and these converts, the Moriscos, were expelled in the early 17th century. Among the surviving monuments are the Cathedral of Córdoba, the Alhambra and the Giralda.
al-aqsa-mosque: The mosque stands on the southern part of the Temple Mount, or Haram al-Sharif, an enclosure that King Herod the Great expanded from 20 BCE during his rebuilding of the Second Jewish Temple. In the late Second Temple period the site held the Royal Stoa, a basilica along the southern wall, which was destroyed with the Temple during the Roman siege of Jerusalem in 70 CE. The Nea Church of Justinian, consecrated in 543, was once thought to have stood here, but remains identified as its were found in the Jewish Quarter in 1973.

According to Islamic tradition, Umar, the second caliph (r. 634–644), built a small prayer hall on the compound. In the reign of Mu'awiya I (r. 661–680) a quadrangular mosque for 3,000 worshippers is recorded. The present mosque was built by the Umayyad caliph Abd al-Malik (r. 685–705), his successor al-Walid I, or both, on the same axis as the Dome of the Rock.

An earthquake destroyed the mosque in 746, and the Abbasid caliph al-Mansur rebuilt it in 758. Al-Mahdi expanded it in 780 to fifteen aisles and a central dome. Another earthquake destroyed it in 1033, and the Fatimid caliph al-Zahir rebuilt it with seven aisles, preserving the outline that survives. The Fatimid caliph al-Mustansir Billah had its facade built in 1065.

After the Crusaders captured Jerusalem in 1099 the mosque served as a palace and as the headquarters of the Knights Templar. Saladin conquered the area in 1187 and restored its use as a mosque. The Ayyubids, Mamluks, Ottomans, the Supreme Muslim Council of British Palestine and the Jordanian administration all later renovated or enlarged it. The dome was destroyed by fire in 1969 and its painted interior was reconstructed using the trateggio technique.

The name al-Masjid al-Aqṣā, 'the furthest mosque', occurs in the Quran's Surah 17 and was first applied to the whole compound, since no buildings stood there then. The building discussed here is the silver-domed congregational mosque, called Jāmiʿ al-Aqṣā or the Qibli Mosque for its place at the southern end of the compound. Medieval writers such as al-Muqaddasi called it al-Mughattâ, 'the covered part'.

The mosque is 83 metres long and 56 metres wide and can hold up to 5,000 worshippers. It has seven aisles.
