Its facade has fourteen stone arches, mostly Romanesque, some made from sculpted material taken from Crusader buildings, and the porch was ordered by al-Mu'azzam Isa in 1217. It has 121 stained glass windows from the Abbasid and Fatimid eras. Unlike the Dome of the Rock, which reflects classical Byzantine architecture, it is characteristic of early Islamic architecture.
al-farabi: Little is known of al-Farabi's life. The accounts of his origins vary and seem to rest on hearsay or guesses, and Arabic biographers of the 12th and 13th centuries had few facts and used invented stories. His full name was Abu Nasr Muhammad ibn Muhammad al-Farabi, sometimes with the family name al-Tarkhani. His birthplace could have been any of several places in Central Asia, then called Khurasan, since farab is a Persian term for land irrigated by springs or a nearby river. Candidates include Farab (Otrar) on the Syr Darya, a village near Türkmenabat and Faryab in present-day Afghanistan.

From incidental accounts it is known that he spent most of his scholarly life in Baghdad with Syriac Christian scholars, among them Yuhanna ibn Haylan, Yahya ibn Adi and Abu Ishaq Ibrahim al-Baghdadi. He later spent time in Damascus and in Egypt before returning to Damascus, where he died in 950–951. His religious affiliation is disputed, and some scholars place him as Sunni and others as Shia or influenced by Shia thought.

Al-Farabi is credited with over one hundred works, among them prolegomena to philosophy and commentaries on Aristotle, including the Nicomachean Ethics. His main influence was the Aristotelian tradition of Alexandria, with elements of Neoplatonism and of Ptolemy's planetary model. In logic he was mainly an Aristotelian but discussed future contingents, the relation of logic to grammar and Stoic forms of inference, and he introduced the concept of the poetic syllogism in a commentary on Aristotle's Poetics. He also wrote on alchemy, in The Necessity of the Art of the Elixir, and was a practical musician and music theorist.

In metaphysics he held that the subject was being as such, related to God only as a principle of absolute being, and Avicenna remarked that he understood Aristotle's Metaphysics only after reading al-Farabi's prolegomenon. His cosmology had the First Cause, by contemplating itself, give rise to a cascade of ten intellects, each bringing a celestial sphere into being, beneath which lies the material world. The process was necessary rather than willed, a view that al-Ghazzali later criticised.

Later writers called al-Farabi the Second Master, with Aristotle the first. He is credited as the first Muslim to present philosophy as a coherent system, and he is called the founder of Islamic political philosophy. Among those he influenced are Avicenna, Averroes, Maimonides and Albertus Magnus. He helped to pass on Aristotle's thought to the Christian West, and he is the only philosopher named in Maimonides's Treatise on Logic.

In Kazakhstan a large university, KazNU, bears his name, and monuments to him stand in Alma-Ata, Shymkent and Turkestan. The 1100th anniversary of his birth was marked in 1975 in Moscow, Alma-Ata and Baghdad, and the asteroid 7057 Al-Fārābī is named after him.
alanya: Alanya lies on the southern coast of Turkey, in Antalya Province, 133 km east of the city of Antalya. It occupies a small peninsula on the Gulf of Antalya, in Pamphylia, between the Taurus Mountains to the north and the Mediterranean, along about 70 km of coastline. This natural strategic position made it a local stronghold for many Mediterranean-based empires, including the Ptolemaic, Seleucid, Roman, Byzantine and Ottoman empires.

Finds in the nearby Karain Cave indicate occupation as far back as the Paleolithic, and evidence shows a port at Syedra, south of the modern city, in the Bronze Age. The city appears in the 4th-century BCE periplus of Pseudo-Scylax, and the castle rock was probably inhabited under the Hittites and the Achaemenid Empire. After Alexander the Great's conquest it was first fortified in the Hellenistic period. Under Ptolemaic rule the port became a popular refuge for Mediterranean pirates. It resisted Antiochus III in 199 BCE but was loyal to the pirate Diodotus Tryphon, who seized the Seleucid crown from 142 to 138 BCE, and Antiochus VII Sidetes completed a new castle and port in 137 BCE.

Its names show its history. It was Korakesion in Greek, from a Luwian word for a protruding city, and Kalonoros under the Byzantine Empire. Its main political importance came in the Middle Ages under the Seljuk Sultanate of Rûm and Alaeddin Kayqubad I, from whom the city takes its name; it became Alaiye. His building campaign produced Alanya Castle, dating from 1226, the Kızıl Kule (Red Tower) and the Tersane (shipyard). In the 13th and 14th centuries Italian traders called the city Candelore or Cardelloro. Mustafa Kemal Atatürk finalised the form Alanya during a visit in 1935. It became a municipality in 1872. After the Treaty of Lausanne in 1923 many of its Christians were resettled in Nea Ionia in Greece.

Alanya is a district and resort city of Antalya Province, with a district population of 364,180 in 2022. Tourism has been the dominant industry since 1958. On the peninsula stands Alanya Castle, a Seljuk citadel built over earlier fortifications, with the Süleymaniye mosque and caravanserai built by the Ottoman ruler Suleiman inside it. Old walls surround much of the eastern peninsula, and within them stand historic villas, most built in the early 19th century. Akşebe Sultan, the castle's first commander under Kayqubad I, is buried in a mausoleum within the walls.
alaska: Alaska lies at the northwest corner of North America, very near to Asia. It borders Canada's Yukon and British Columbia to the east, with the Pacific Ocean to the south, the Bering Sea, Bering Strait and Chukchi Sea to the west and the Arctic Ocean to the north. About 500 miles of Canadian territory separate it from Washington. In the Bering Strait the Russian Big Diomede Island and the Alaskan Little Diomede Island are only 3 miles apart. Its coastline is longer than that of all the other U.S. states combined. The name derives from an Aleut idiom, alaxsxaq, meaning 'the mainland'.

Indigenous peoples occupied Alaska for thousands of years before European contact, and linguistic and DNA studies support the settlement of North America by way of the Bering land bridge. At the Upward Sun River site the remains of a six-week-old infant belonged to a population genetically separate from other Native groups, which the archaeologist Ben Potter named Ancient Beringian. The Tlingit and Haida lived in the southeast, and all three of these peoples and others of the Pacific Northwest Coast suffered smallpox outbreaks from the late 18th century, the worst in the 1830s and 1860s.

The Russian Empire began to colonise the area in the 18th century, establishing Russian America. The expense and difficulty of holding it led to its sale to the United States in 1867 for US$7.2 million. Alaska became a territory on 11 May 1912 and the 49th state on 3 January 1959.

Alaska is a state of the United States, with Juneau as its capital and Anchorage as its most populous city. Juneau is on the mainland but has no road connection to the rest of the North American highway system. More than half the state is federally owned, in national forests, national parks and wildlife refuges. The Alaska Native Heritage Center celebrates the state's 11 cultural groups.
alatri: Alatri is a town and comune of the province of Frosinone in the region of Lazio, Italy. Its Latin name was Aletrium. The area of the modern town was settled as early as the 2nd millennium BCE, and the ancient town was a city of the Hernici. A hill in the centre of the city was adopted as its citadel.

Aletrium was a town of the Hernici which, together with Veroli, Anagni and Ferentino, formed a defensive league against the Volsci and the Samnites around 550 BCE. In 530 BCE the Hernici allied with the Rome of Tarquinius Superbus, which confirms the Etruscan influence in the area that archaeology also shows. Alatri is said to have been defeated by Rome in 306 BCE and forced to accept citizenship. In the time of Cicero it was a municipium and remained one throughout the imperial period.

After the fall of the Western Roman Empire the city decayed, and the Christian bishop was the only respected authority. In 543, during the Gothic Wars, Totila's troops sacked and destroyed Alatri. In the 12th century it became an important stronghold of the popes when Rome was unsafe for them. The following century it became a free commune under the authority of the bishops and the pope, governed by consuls until 1241, when a podestà was introduced. In the 15th century it began to lose its freedom, and after the short rule of Filippo Maria Visconti in 1434 it had to accept papal suzerainty. Spanish soldiers occupied it in 1556, and it became part of Italy in 1870.

Alatri has about 30,000 inhabitants and is known for its megalithic acropolis. Well-preserved polygonal fortifications of local limestone, probably up to about 9 m high, survive around the city, and on the citadel hill huge terrace walls over 15 m high enclose an area of 220 by 100 m. The Cathedral of San Paolo is documented since 930, and the Collegiata of Santa Maria Maggiore was largely rebuilt in the 13th century.
albert-einstein: Einstein was born in Ulm on 14 March 1879, a subject of the Kingdom of Württemberg in the German Empire. His parents, Hermann Einstein and Pauline Koch, were secular Ashkenazi Jews. The family moved to Munich in 1880, where his father and uncle Jakob founded a company making electrical equipment. His parents worried that he had a learning disability because he was slow to talk, and a compass his father gave him when he was five began a lifelong fascination with electromagnetism. He found the rote learning of the Luitpold Gymnasium harmful to creativity and left it in December 1894 to join his family in Italy.

He renounced his German citizenship on 28 January 1896, avoiding conscription, and enrolled that year at the Swiss federal polytechnic school in Zurich, graduating in 1900. He gained Swiss citizenship a year later and secured a permanent position at the Swiss Patent Office in Bern.

His first paper, on capillary attraction, appeared in 1901. In 1905, sometimes called his annus mirabilis, he published papers on the photoelectric effect, on Brownian motion, which showed that the movement could be taken as firm evidence that molecules exist, and on special relativity, and demonstrated that mass and energy are equivalent. The paper on the electrodynamics of moving bodies was received on 30 June 1905 and reconciled Maxwell's equations with Newtonian mechanics.

In 1915 he proposed a general theory of relativity that extended his mechanics to gravitation, and a paper of the following year introduced the cosmological constant and is regarded as the first step in modern theoretical cosmology. In 1917 he introduced spontaneous and stimulated emission, the latter the core mechanism behind the laser. In his last years he objected to the randomness of quantum theory and tried unsuccessfully to devise a unified field theory, which left him increasingly isolated from mainstream physics.

In 1914 Einstein moved to Berlin, and in 1917 he became director of the Kaiser Wilhelm Institute for Physics. He was visiting the United States in 1933 when Adolf Hitler came to power; horrified by the Nazi persecution of Jews, he stayed, and became an American citizen in 1940. He died on 18 April 1955.

The Nobel committee found that no nomination in 1921 met Alfred Nobel's criteria, so the prize in physics was carried forward and awarded to Einstein in 1922 for his discovery of the law of the photoelectric effect. The element einsteinium was named after him in 1955, and Time named him Person of the Century in 1999.
albertus-magnus: Albertus Magnus was probably born before 1200, since well-attested evidence shows he was over 80 when he died in 1280. Two later sources give his age as about 87, which led to 1193 being commonly given as his birth year, but that information cannot be confirmed. He was probably born in Lauingen, in what is now Bavaria, since he called himself Albert of Lauingen. He was probably educated chiefly at the University of Padua, where he was taught Aristotle's writings. In 1223 (or 1229) he joined the Dominican Order and studied theology at Bologna and elsewhere.

Albert taught for several years as lecturer at the Dominican house in Cologne, and also in Regensburg, Freiburg, Strasbourg and Hildesheim. In 1245 he became master of theology under Guerric of Saint-Quentin, the first German Dominican to do so, and taught at the University of Paris, where Thomas Aquinas began to study under him. He was the first to comment on virtually all of Aristotle's writings, which led him to the teachings of Avicenna and Averroes. In 1254 he became provincial of the Dominican Order. At the General Chapter at Valenciennes in 1259 he helped set up a program of studies that made philosophy part of Dominican training.

In 1260 Pope Alexander IV made him bishop of Regensburg, an office he resigned after three years. In 1263 Pope Urban IV relieved him of his duties as bishop and asked him to preach the Eighth Crusade in German-speaking countries. He then became known as a mediator, and in 1258 his verdict, the Große Schied, ended a conflict between the citizens of Cologne and the archbishop.

Albert's writings, collected in 1899, filled thirty-eight volumes, on topics from logic and theology to botany, astronomy, mineralogy and zoology. He believed that Aristotle's approach to natural philosophy posed no obstacle to a Christian view of the natural order. His books on botany, zoology and minerals drew on ancient sources and on his own empirical investigations. In embryology it has been claimed that little of value was written after Aristotle until Albert, who identified organs within eggs. Many alchemical works were later falsely attributed to him, and there is scant evidence that he performed alchemical experiments himself.

Albert died on 15 November 1280 in the Dominican convent in Cologne. His relics are in a Roman sarcophagus in the crypt of St. Andrew's Church there. He was beatified in 1622, canonized and proclaimed a Doctor of the Church on 16 December 1931 by Pope Pius XI, and named patron saint of natural scientists in 1941. His feast day is 15 November.
albi: The first settlement at Albi dates to the Bronze Age. After the Roman conquest of Gaul in 51 BCE the town became the Civitas Albigensium, the territory of the Albigeois. Excavations have found no traces of Roman buildings, which suggests a modest settlement. In 584 Gregory of Tours reported that most of the townsfolk died of plague. In 1040 the town expanded and built the Pont Vieux, or Old Bridge, and its new quarters show considerable urban growth. It grew rich from trade and from the tolls charged to travellers on the bridge.

In 1208 the Pope and the French king joined forces against the Cathars, who held their own version of ascetic Christian dualism, which the Catholic Church considered a dangerous heresy. Repression was severe, many Cathars were burnt at the stake, and the area, until then virtually independent, was afterwards annexed by the French Crown. Late in the 13th century the bishop Bernard de Castanet completed the Palais de la Berbie, a fortress-like episcopal palace, and ordered the building of Sainte-Cécile cathedral from 1282. Trade in woad then made the town prosperous, and the fine Renaissance houses show the fortunes of its woad merchants. A small medieval Jewish community was annihilated in the 1320s during the Shepherds' Crusade.

Albi is the prefecture of the Tarn department, on the river Tarn 85 km northeast of Toulouse, and the seat of an archbishop. Along with Toulouse and Montauban it is one of the main cities built in Languedoc red brick. Its episcopal city was added to the UNESCO World Heritage list in 2010.

Sainte-Cécile is a masterpiece of Southern Gothic, built between the 13th and 15th centuries, with an austere defensive exterior and a rich interior. Its rood screen is carved in the Flamboyant Gothic style and carries over 200 polychrome statues. The Pont Vieux, 151 metres long on eight arches, is still in use after almost a millennium. The Toulouse-Lautrec Museum in the Palais de la Berbie holds more than 1,000 works by the painter Henri de Toulouse-Lautrec, who was born in Albi in 1864.
alessandro-manzoni: Alessandro Manzoni was born in Milan on 7 March 1785. His maternal grandfather was the philosopher Cesare Beccaria, and his biological father was probably Giovanni Verri rather than Pietro Manzoni. His parents separated in 1792, and from the age of six he was schooled in religious boarding schools run by the Somaschi and Barnabite fathers. He was drawn early to poetry and to ideals of liberty and reason, and his poem The Triumph of Liberty (1801) praised the French Revolution.

After his father's death in 1807 he joined his mother's household at Auteuil and met the Idéologues, including Claude Charles Fauriel. In 1808 he married Henriette Blondel, a Calvinist banker's daughter who became a Roman Catholic in 1810. That year Manzoni passed through a religious crisis that took him from agnosticism to an austere Catholicism. His Sacred Hymns appeared in 1815.

Manzoni began Fermo e Lucia on 24 April 1821, after reading the novels of Walter Scott in French translation, and finished the first manuscript in September 1823. The reshaped novel, The Betrothed (I promessi sposi), was published a volume a year in 1825–1827. It follows two ordinary fiancés, Renzo Tramaglino and Lucia Mondella, through famine, war and plague and through corruption in Church and State in 17th-century Lombardy under Spanish rule. Real figures appear, among them Cardinal Federico Borromeo and the outlaw called the Unnamed, historically identified with Francesco Bernardino Visconti.

The novel went through 68 editions and sold over 60,000 copies in fourteen years. Manzoni's tragedy Adelchi (1822), on Charlemagne's overthrow of the Lombard domination in Italy, carried veiled allusions to Austrian rule. Later he wrote mainly essays, above all on language. In 1868 he reported to the minister Emilio Broglio, proposing that Florentine be taught in schools. He supported Italian unification and became a senator in February 1860.

Manzoni outlived his first wife, who died on 25 December 1833, his second wife, Teresa Borri, six of his children and his closest friends. His eldest son, Pier Luigi, died on 28 April 1873. Manzoni had fallen on 6 January while leaving the San Fedele church, and he died of cerebral meningitis, a complication of the blow to his head, on 22 May 1873. His funeral was held in Milan Cathedral with almost royal pomp, and he was buried in the Monumental Cemetery of Milan.

He is counted with Ugo Foscolo and Giacomo Leopardi as one of the three crowns of Italian Romanticism. The Betrothed is a symbol of the Risorgimento for its patriotic message, and it was a milestone in the development of the modern and unified Italian language.
aleutian-islands: The Aleutian Islands are a chain of 14 main volcanic islands and 55 smaller ones. They extend westward roughly 1,200 miles (1,900 km) from the Alaska Peninsula towards Kamchatka and separate the Bering Sea to the north from the Pacific Ocean to the south. The 57 volcanoes of the islands form the northernmost part of the Pacific Ring of Fire. Before 1867 the islands were known as the Catherine Archipelago. The climate is oceanic, with heavy rainfall and almost constant fog, and the vast majority of the chain has no native trees.

The first occupants probably arrived following Beringian migrations. The earliest archaeological sites, on Unalaska, date to about 9,000 years ago, those on Adak to about 6,000 years ago, and the western islands were settled last, about 2,500 years ago. The native people call themselves Unangan and are generally known as Aleut. They developed a culture tied to marine resources, with boat building, tools for fishing and sea-mammal hunting, and noted basketry and weaving.

In 1741 Vitus Bering and Aleksei Chirikov sailed from Russia on a voyage of discovery, and after a storm separated them Chirikov found several eastern islands and Bering several western ones. Bering was shipwrecked and died on the Commander Islands, and his survivors reported that the islands were rich in fur-bearing animals. Siberian fur hunters moved eastward across the chain, and the islands belonged to Russia until the Alaska Purchase of 1867. Grigory Shelikhov founded a company in the 1780s based on the systematic exploitation of the indigenous peoples, with sporadic conflict such as the Awa'uq Massacre. The first Orthodox missionaries arrived in 1793.

On 3 June 1942 Japanese forces invaded Attu and Kiska, the only invasions of the United States during the war. The United States moved over 800 civilians to camps in the Alaska Panhandle, and more than 90 Americans were taken to Japan as prisoners. American forces retook Attu in May 1943. The August 1943 landing on Kiska found the island already evacuated by its Japanese force of 5,183 men, though 313 Allied men died there from accidents. The United States tested nuclear weapons underground on Amchitka from 1965 to 1971.

Most of the islands belong to the U.S. state of Alaska, while the Commander Islands, farther west, belong to Kamchatka Krai in Russia. The 2020 census recorded 7,152 people on the islands, 4,254 of them in Unalaska, the main settlement. Fishing is the main economic activity, and nearly all the islands are protected within the Alaska Maritime National Wildlife Refuge. Large seabird colonies breed there, and sea otters help keep kelp forests along the coasts.
alexander-dubcek: Alexander Dubček was born in Uhrovec, Czechoslovakia, on 27 November 1921. When he was three his family moved to the Soviet Union in search of work and a better life, and he spent most of his childhood in Interhelpo, an Esperantist industrial cooperative in Kyrgyzstan. In 1933 the family moved to Gorky. In 1938 they chose to return to Czechoslovakia rather than renounce their citizenship. At 17 he joined the then-illegal Communist Party of Slovakia. He fought against the wartime pro-German Slovak state of Jozef Tiso and, in August 1944, joined the Jan Žižka partisan brigade during the Slovak National Uprising, in which his brother died.

After the Communist Party took power in 1948, Dubček rose through party posts in Trenčín, Bratislava and Banská Bystrica. He studied in the Soviet Union from 1955 to 1958 and was transferred to Prague in 1960. There he worked on the commissions that rehabilitated victims of repression in 1962–1963, and learning of the mechanisms of repression, he later said, was a watershed that dedicated him to reform. The Czechoslovak economy had begun to plateau in the early 1960s, and reformers concluded that the country had fallen behind the rest of the world.

Dubček was First Secretary of the party from January 1968 to April 1969 and became best known for the slogan Socialism with a human face. His reforms accelerated cultural and economic liberalisation, and culture changed most quickly. On the night of 20–21 August 1968 Soviet-led Warsaw Pact forces, reportedly about half a million troops, invaded Czechoslovakia. Albania, Romania and East Germany did not take part.

The invasion was meant to enable a coup by conservatives, but it could not succeed because of the lack of a viable pro-Soviet leadership and the popularity of Dubček. He was forced to resign in April 1969 and succeeded by Gustáv Husák, and was expelled from the party in 1970.

Dubček then lived as a nonperson whose very mention was banned, in Bratislava. In November 1989, during the Velvet Revolution, he spoke to a crowd at the trial of the Bratislava Five on 14 November, was briefly arrested on 17 November at the students' march in Prague, and appeared on 23 November in Bratislava.

He became Chairman of the federal parliament from 1989 to 1992, and the European Parliament awarded him the Sakharov Prize in 1989. He died on 7 November 1992 of injuries from a car crash on 1 September on the D1 motorway near Humpolec. A later investigation ruled the cause aquaplaning at excessive speed, though his son Pavol remained sceptical. Andrei Sakharov wrote that the breath of freedom under Dubček was a prologue to the peaceful revolutions in eastern Europe.
alexander-hamilton: Hamilton was born on 11 January 1755 or 1757 in Charlestown, the capital of Nevis in the British Leeward Islands. He and his older brother, James Jr., were born out of wedlock to Rachel Lavien, a married woman of half-British and half-Huguenot descent, and James A. Hamilton, a Scotsman. He was orphaned as a child, taken in by a merchant, and given a scholarship to King's College (now Columbia University) in New York City.

In 1775, after the fighting at Lexington and Concord, he joined a New York volunteer company and was elected an officer. In 1776 he raised the New York Provincial Company of Artillery and was appointed captain. He served for four years as aide-de-camp to George Washington and fought at the Siege of Yorktown.

Hamilton resigned his commission in March 1782 and was appointed to the Congress of the Confederation, whose want of power he had criticised. He founded the Bank of New York, led the Annapolis Convention of 1786 and was a delegate to the Philadelphia Convention, which drafted the Constitution. He wrote 51 of the 85 installments of The Federalist Papers.

Washington appointed him first secretary of the treasury, and he was sworn in on 11 September 1789. He argued that the Constitution's implied powers allowed the First Bank of the United States, funded by a tariff on imports and a whiskey tax, to take on the states' war debts. His views became the basis of the Federalist Party, opposed by the Democratic-Republican Party under Thomas Jefferson. He resigned in 1795 and resumed his law practice.

Hamilton opposed Aaron Burr's candidacy for governor of New York in 1804. Letters published in the Albany Register alleged that he had expressed a despicable opinion of Burr, and Burr demanded an apology. Hamilton refused because he could not recall such an insult, and a duel was arranged. It took place at Weehawken, New Jersey, on 11 July 1804. Hamilton was mortally wounded and died the next day.

His interpretations in The Federalist Papers remain highly influential and are cited in scholarly studies and court decisions. His dispute with Jefferson over a national bank was addressed in McCulloch v. Maryland, which largely adopted Hamilton's view.
alexander-ii-of-russia: Alexander Nikolayevich was born in Moscow, the eldest son of Nicholas I of Russia and Charlotte of Prussia. He became Tsesarevich in 1825, when his father took the throne. Under Nicholas the intellectual atmosphere of Saint Petersburg suppressed freedom of thought. The poet Vasily Zhukovsky supervised his education. In 1837 he toured twenty provinces of Russia and was the first Romanov heir to visit Siberia.
He met Princess Marie of Hesse in Darmstadt on a tour of Europe, and they married in Saint Petersburg on 16 April 1841. The marriage produced six sons and two daughters.

Alexander became emperor on 2 March 1855. On 15 January 1856 he took Russia out of the Crimean War on the unfavourable terms of the Treaty of Paris, which cost the Black Sea Fleet. This gave him room for domestic reform: the Edict of Emancipation of 1861, which abolished serfdom, and changes to the courts, local self-government, censorship, schools and the army. Many reforms met intense backlash and were cut back, and after an assassination attempt in 1866 he moved towards a more conservative stance.

In 1863 a Polish uprising led him to strip Poland of its separate constitution and incorporate the kingdom directly into the Russian Empire. In 1867 he sold Alaska to the United States. The Russo-Turkish War of 1877–1878 brought independence to Bulgaria, Montenegro, Romania and Serbia. He also approved military plans in the Caucasus that culminated in the Circassian genocide.

After a last attempt on his life in February 1880, Count Loris-Melikov was given extraordinary powers against the revolutionaries, and his proposals called for a form of parliamentary body. On 13 March 1881 (1 March in the old-style calendar) Alexander was assassinated in Saint Petersburg. A bomb thrown by Nikolai Rysakov of the Narodnaya Volya damaged his carriage but left him unhurt, and a second member, Ignacy Hryniewiecki, then threw something at his feet.

Alexander had approved Loris-Melikov's plans as the first step towards a constitution. His successor, Alexander III, on the advice of Konstantin Pobedonostsev, abandoned them. The assassination brought suppression of civil liberties, use of the Okhrana secret police, and anti-Jewish pogroms and the May Laws.
alexander-the-great: Alexander was born in Pella, the capital of Macedon, probably on 20 July 356 BCE, the son of Philip II and his fourth wife, Olympias, daughter of King Neoptolemus I of Epirus. According to the biographer Plutarch, Olympias dreamed that a thunderbolt struck her womb, and Plutarch suggested that Zeus was Alexander's father. Alexander claimed descent from Heracles and Perseus through his father and from Achilles through his mother. Aristotle tutored him until he was 16, after which he governed as regent while Philip fought the Thracians.

Philip was assassinated by his chief bodyguard Pausanias, probably on 25 October 336 BCE, and the army proclaimed the 20-year-old Alexander king. He executed his cousin Amyntas IV and two Macedonian princes, destroyed the city of Thebes and took over the League of Corinth. In 334 BCE he launched a pan-Hellenic invasion of the Achaemenid Persian Empire. After conquering Asia Minor he won decisive battles at Issus and Gaugamela, overthrew Darius III and took the whole empire.

In 326 BCE he invaded India and defeated the king Porus at the Battle of the Hydaspes, but facing a mutiny he turned back at the Beas River. According to Curtius, he slaughtered the entire population of Massaga. At Opis his troops mutinied again, resenting his adoption of Persian customs and his promotion of Persian officers.

Alexander died in Babylon on 10 or 11 June 323 BCE, at age 32. Plutarch describes a fever that worsened until he could not speak, while Diodorus tells of pain after a large bowl of unmixed wine. Civil wars then broke out and the Diadochi broke up the empire, beginning the Hellenistic period. He founded more than twenty cities, the most prominent being Alexandria in Egypt. The works of those who knew him, including Ptolemy and Nearchus, are lost, and Arrian, who drew on Ptolemy and Aristobulus, is generally considered the most reliable of the later writers.
algeria: Algeria is the largest country in Africa and the Mediterranean basin, covering 2,381,741 square kilometres. The Sahara covers most of it. In the north, the Tell Atlas and the Saharan Atlas form two parallel sets of reliefs, and the area from the coast to the Tell Atlas is fertile; south of it lies steppe, then the desert. The highest point is Mount Tahat, at 3,003 metres, in the Hoggar Mountains of the central Sahara. About 90% of Algerians live in the northern coastal area, and Algiers, Oran, Constantine and Annaba are the main cities.

Early finds show that hominins lived on the Mediterranean fringe of northern Africa earlier than previously thought. Neolithic life, richly depicted in the Tassili n'Ajjer paintings, predominated until the classical period. The Carthaginians established settlements on the coast, and by 600 BCE a Phoenician presence existed at places such as Icosium, now Algiers, and Hippo Regius.

They avoided conquering the strong Berber tribes of the interior, collected tribute and traded, and the Berbers supplied them with goods, slaves and skilled cavalry. Amazigh societies, among them the Numidians, whose kingdom became one of the earliest major states in the region, were also shaped by Roman, Vandal and Byzantine influences.

From the 7th century the spread of Islam and the arrival of Arab tribes gradually transformed the region, and from the 8th to the 15th centuries local Islamic dynasties ruled. The Regency of Algiers, established in 1516, became a largely autonomous state owing nominal allegiance to the Ottoman Empire. France invaded in 1830 and formally annexed Algeria in 1848, though it was not fully conquered until 1903. French rule brought mass European settlement that displaced the local population, and by the mid-1870s indigenous Algerians had declined by up to a third through warfare, disease and starvation.

Resistance to French colonisation ran from the campaigns of Emir Abdelkader and the Mokrani Revolt to the nationalist movements of the 20th century. The Sétif and Guelma massacre in 1945 catalysed the resistance that led to the outbreak of the Algerian War in 1954, and Algeria gained independence in 1962. A civil war lasted from 1992 to 2002. The country is a semi-presidential republic with a population of about 47 million. Its official languages are Arabic and Amazigh, most people speak Algerian Arabic, and Sunni Islam is the official religion.
ali-adil-shah-ii: Ali Adil Shah II was the eighth sultan of Bijapur. He came to the throne on the death of Mohammed Adil Shah on 4 November 1656, through the efforts of the prime minister Khan Muhammad and of the queen Badi Sahiba, a sister of the Qutb Shah of Golkonda. The Mughal emperor Shah Jahan, who wished to annex Bijapur, found a pretext in doubts about Ali's parentage and, at the plea of his son Aurangzeb, sanctioned an invasion, although Bijapur was an independent ally of the Mughals and not their vassal. Aurangzeb had to raise the siege and hurry north for the war of succession to the Mughal throne.

With the accession of a young ruler, disorder began in the Karnataka, where the Nayaks tried to recover their former lands; Bangalore was Bijapur's administrative headquarters for controlling these feudatories. At court the struggle of factions for supremacy reached its height, and Aurangzeb intrigued with the Bijapur nobles and won over most of them. Shivaji meanwhile took more and more Bijapur territory, and his diplomacy prevented any coalition of the Mughals and Bijapur against him.

Through the sixteen years of his reign Ali fought both the Mughals and the Marathas, and he three times repulsed Mughal invasions. The reign was also marked by developments in Persian and Deccani literature and the fine arts. Beside the poet laureate Nusrati, the historian Nurullah wrote under his patronage a history known as the Tarikh-i Ali Adil Shah.

Ali died on 24 November 1672. By then the kingdom had lost most of its important territories, shrinking as Shivaji's kingdom grew, and the reign is seen as marking the decline of Bijapur. He was buried in Ali Ka Rouza, the monument at Bijapur known as the Bara Kaman.
altan-khan: Altan was the second son of Bars Bolud Jinong and a grandson of Dayan Khan. After Dayan Khan the Mongols formed six tümen divided into a Left Wing under the Great Khan and a Right Wing under Altan's father, who held the office of jinong, or vice-regent. Altan ruled the Tümed, whose pastures lay north of the border with Shanxi. When his elder brother Gün Bilig died in 1542, Altan became the effective leader of the Right Wing. After the death of Bodi Alagh Khan in 1547 he forced the new khagan, Darayisung Küdeng Khan, to flee eastward, and in 1551 Darayisung compromised by granting him the title Gegeen Khan.

Altan wanted to trade horses for Chinese farm produce and textiles, but the Ming court, suspicious of him, repeatedly refused and sometimes killed his envoys. He raided northern China in 1529, 1530 and 1542, and in 1550 crossed gaps in the Great Wall and besieged Beijing, setting its suburbs on fire. He strengthened his Tümed base by settling Chinese refugees there and kept a network of Ming conspirators led by Zhao Quan, a disciple of the White Lotus. In 1552 he gained control of the remains of Karakorum.

In 1570 his grandson Daičing Ejei Taiji defected to the Ming after a family quarrel. Ministers of the Longqing Emperor proposed that Altan accept a Ming title and hand over Zhao Quan in return for his grandson and trading rights. Altan agreed; Zhao and his fellow conspirators were executed, Altan was made Shunyi prince and his capital was renamed Guihua. The American Orientalist Owen Lattimore writes that the Mongols were nominally vassals, but that the Ming was eager to please them and the arrangement was more or less of benefit to both.

Altan first invited Sonam Gyatso in 1569; the lama accepted a second invitation in 1577, and Altan later had Thegchen Chonkhor, Mongolia's first monastery, built where they met. Sonam Gyatso declared Altan a reincarnation of Kublai Khan. One reason for adopting Buddhism was a fear among the Mongol elite that the peace of 1571 would spread Chinese cultural influence. Laws set out by Sonam Gyatso and instituted by Altan forbade blood sacrifices and the burning of widows. Altan died on 13 January 1582, aged 74 or 75, and his son Sengge Düüreng succeeded him as Shunyi prince. His great-grandson Yonten Gyatso was chosen as the 4th Dalai Lama in 1601.
americas: The Americas are a landmass made up of North America and South America. Together with their islands they cover 8% of Earth's surface and 28.4% of its land area, and they make up most of the land in the Western Hemisphere. The mainland extends about 14,000 km from north to south, and its climate ranges from arctic tundra in northern Canada, Greenland and Alaska to tropical rainforest in Central America and South America. A long chain of mountains, the American Cordillera, runs along the west coast, while the flatter east is dominated by river basins such as the Amazon and the Mississippi. The two continents were joined by the Isthmus of Panama by about three million years ago.

Humans first settled the Americas from Asia between 20,000 and 16,000 years ago, though the dates and routes are subject to research. The pre-Columbian era saw urban settlement, agriculture and monumental architecture in Mesoamerica, among the Olmec, Zapotec, Aztec and Maya, and among the Andean civilizations. Norse settlements in Greenland, and perhaps on the mainland, were later abandoned.

The voyages of Christopher Columbus from 1492 to 1504 brought permanent contact with Europe and began a period of exploration, conquest and colonisation. Large numbers of Indigenous people were enslaved, and diseases from Europe and West Africa devastated them. Decolonisation began with the American Revolution in the 1770s and largely ended with the Spanish–American War in the late 1890s. The name America was first recorded in 1507, on a world map by Martin Waldseemüller, and is generally thought to derive from Amerigo Vespucci.

The Americas have more than a billion inhabitants and 35 sovereign states, together with dependent territories of Denmark, France, the Netherlands, the United Kingdom and the United States. The legacy of European settlement is a set of shared cultural traits, most notably Christianity and the use of West European languages, chiefly Spanish, English, Portuguese and French. The population descends from Indigenous peoples and from people of European, African and Asian ancestry, along with people of mixed ancestry.
amsterdam: Amsterdam lies in the province of North Holland, in the western Netherlands, at an elevation of about 2 metres below sea level. The river Amstel ends in the city centre and connects to a large number of canals that eventually terminate in the IJ. The surrounding land is flat and formed of large polders, and the city is connected to the North Sea by the North Sea Canal. More than 100 kilometres of canals run through it, most of them navigable. The three main ones are the Prinsengracht, the Herengracht and the Keizersgracht.

Farmers settled around the area of the later city about three millennia ago, along the prehistoric IJ and upstream on its tributary the Amstel. A permanent settlement was not possible until water issues were controlled, because the river mouth and banks were too wet. Amsterdam was founded at the mouth of the Amstel, which was dammed to control flooding, and it began as a small fishing village in the 12th century. Its population was around 1,000 in 1300. It grew in the 15th and 16th centuries, mainly through the Baltic grain trade after the Burgundian victory in the Dutch–Hanseatic War in 1441.

The population then rose sharply during the Dutch Revolt. Many people from the Southern Netherlands fled north, especially after Antwerp fell to Spanish forces in 1585, and Jews from Spain, Portugal and Eastern Europe, Germans and Scandinavians also settled there. The population more than doubled between 1585 and 1610, stood at about 50,000 in 1600 and reached 200,000 in the 1660s. It then stabilised around 240,000 for most of the 18th century. The Amsterdam Stock Exchange was founded in 1602. In the 19th and 20th centuries the city expanded, and new neighbourhoods and suburbs were built.

Amsterdam is the capital and largest city of the Netherlands, though it is not the seat of government, which is in The Hague. Its 17th-century canal belt, the grachten, is a UNESCO World Heritage Site and preserves narrow canal houses with gabled façades. The Rijksmuseum, opened in 1885, holds Dutch Golden Age art, and the Stedelijk Museum opened in 1895. The city has two universities, the University of Amsterdam and the Vrije Universiteit Amsterdam, and hosted the Summer Olympics in 1928.
andhra-mahabharatam: Nannaya began the translation from Sanskrit at the request of the king, and his part marks the earliest known beginning of a written literary tradition in Telugu. It is composed in the Champu style and is so polished that several scholars think it probable that literary works existed in Telugu before him. No such writings have been found, apart from references to songs and poems and some verses in inscriptions, and Telugu tradition honours him as the Adi Kavi, the first poet.

Tikkana, who lived from 1205 to 1288, was born into a Niyogi Brahmin family and was a minister of the Nellore Chola ruler Manumasiddhi II. Errana, also called Yerrapragada, was a poet at the court of King Prolaya Vema Reddy, who reigned from 1325 to 1353 and founded the Reddy dynasty; he bore the titles Prabandha-parameshvara and Shambhudasudu, servant of Shiva.

The work is not a stanza-by-stanza translation but a Telugu rendering that keeps the core narrative of the Mahabharata. Nannaya wrote the Adi Parvam, the Sabha Parvam and part of the Aranya Parvam, the Book of the Forest. Tikkana wrote the fifteen books from the Virata Parvam to the Svargarohana Parvam but did not touch the half-finished third book, because it was considered inauspicious to take up what Nannaya had left incomplete. It remained unfinished for more than a century until Errana completed it. He began his portion in the style of Nannaya and ended it in the style of Tikkana, as a bridge between the two.

The Sanskrit epic is reckoned at 100 parvas and 100,000 verses. In Telugu Nannaya arranged it in eighteen parvas, divided into chapters called ashvasas, without the subdivision into upaparvas, and left out the Harivamsa; Tikkana followed his arrangement, and Errana wrote the Harivamsa as a separate work.

The three poets are revered by later Telugu poets as the Kavitrayam, the trinity of poets, and became models for all who followed. Though written by three hands over about two and a half centuries, the work is read as a single book, as if one poet had composed it in one period. Errana went on to translate the Ramayana from Sanskrit and to write an independent work, the Nrusimhapuranamu.
angola: Angola covers 1,246,700 square kilometres on the western coast of Southern Africa, making it the seventh-largest country in Africa. It borders Namibia, Zambia and the Democratic Republic of the Congo, and its province of Cabinda is an exclave on the Atlantic coast. Luanda, the capital, lies on the coast in the north-west. Angola has four natural harbours: Luanda, Lobito, Moçâmedes and Tômbua. Like the rest of tropical Africa it has alternating rainy and dry seasons, and the dry season is known as the cacimbo.

Before the Bantu migrations the region was populated by nomadic Khoi and San hunter-gatherers. In the first millennium BCE Bantu peoples arriving from the north displaced them and introduced bananas, taro and large cattle herds. States were formed by the 13th century, and the Kingdom of Kongo achieved hegemony from the 14th century. To its south lay Ndongo and Matamba, and the title ngola, held by the kings of Ndongo and Matamba, gave the Portuguese the name Angola. The Portuguese established relations with Kongo in 1483, and Diogo Cão reached the area in 1484.

Paulo Dias de Novais founded São Paulo de Loanda in 1575 with a hundred families of settlers and four hundred soldiers, and Benguela was fortified in 1587. Kongo fought three wars against the Portuguese, ending in the Portuguese conquest of Ndongo. The colony did not reach its present borders until the early 20th century, and met strong resistance from groups such as the Cuamato, the Kwanyama and the Mbunda.

After an anti-colonial struggle from 1961 to 1974, Angola became independent in 1975 as a one-party republic and at once fell into a civil war. The ruling MPLA, backed by the Soviet Union and Cuba, fought the National Union for the Total Independence of Angola, supported by the United States and South Africa, and the National Liberation Front of Angola, backed by Zaire. The civil war ended in 2002, and the peace allowed the resettlement of 4 million displaced persons.

The 2010 constitution made the leader of the winning party in parliamentary elections president, so that there are no separate presidential elections. Oil and diamonds have been the most important resources since independence. Angola had 36,604,681 inhabitants at the 2024 census. Portuguese is the official language and is spoken natively by 45.5 per cent, and Umbundu, Kimbundu and Kikongo are the most widely spoken indigenous languages.
arabic-language: Arabic is classified as a Central Semitic language of the Afroasiatic family. Arabia had a wide variety of Semitic languages in antiquity, among them Ancient South Arabian languages in the southwest, Dadanitic and Taymanitic in the oases of northern Hejaz and Hasaitic in the east. Safaitic and Hismaic, attested on the northwestern frontier, share important features with later forms of Arabic, and scholars theorise that they are early forms of it, to be counted as Old Arabic. Linguists generally believe that Old Arabic, a collection of related dialects, first emerged during the Iron Age.

Classical Arabic, the modern Arabic varieties and the Safaitic and Hismaic inscriptions share features found in no other Central Semitic language, evidence of descent from a hypothetical ancestor, Proto-Arabic. Because several Arabic varieties keep features that Classical Arabic lacks, the vernaculars cannot descend from Classical Arabic, which is a sister language rather than their direct ancestor.

Arabic usually means Standard Arabic, which Western linguists divide into Classical Arabic and Modern Standard Arabic. Classical Arabic is the language of the Quran, used from Pre-Islamic Arabia to the Abbasid Caliphate, and follows the norms set by classical grammarians such as Sibawayh and the vocabulary of classical dictionaries such as the Lisān al-ʻArab. Modern Standard Arabic largely follows its grammar and vocabulary but has taken new vocabulary for concepts of the industrial and post-industrial era. Alongside it stand regional vernacular dialects, usually acquired in families, which are not necessarily mutually intelligible. Educated Arabs speak both, a situation called diglossia.

Arabic has a root-and-pattern morphology. A root of usually three bare consonants is fitted into a pattern to form words: from k-t-b, meaning write, come katabtu, I wrote, kitābun, book, and kātibun, writer. It is written with the Arabic alphabet, an abjad that runs from right to left and derives from the Aramaic through Nabatean.

During the Middle Ages Arabic was a major vehicle of culture and learning, especially in science, mathematics and philosophy, and many European languages borrowed words from it. The influence is seen mainly in Spanish, and less in Portuguese, Catalan and Sicilian, owing to the long Arabic cultural and linguistic presence in southern Iberia in the Al-Andalus era. Maltese is a Semitic language that developed from a dialect of Arabic and is written in the Latin alphabet.

Persian, Turkish, Hindustani, Malay, Hausa and Swahili are among the languages most markedly influenced. The lexicographic tradition lasted about a millennium before the modern period: the Kitāb al-ʿAyn of the 8th century is considered the first lexicon to include all Arabic roots, and Ibn Manzur's Lisān al-ʿArab of 1290 gives 9,273 roots. Arabic is one of the official languages of the United Nations and the liturgical language of Islam.
archimedes: The details of Archimedes's life are obscure. Because John Tzetzes states that he lived 75 years before his death in 212 BCE, he is estimated to have been born around 287 BCE in the seaport of Syracuse, Sicily. In the Sand-Reckoner he gives his father's name as Phidias, an astronomer. Plutarch wrote that he was related to King Hiero II of Syracuse, while Cicero and Silius Italicus suggest humble origins. His works, addressed to Dositheus of Pelusium and to Eratosthenes of Cyrene, suggest that he kept up relations with scholars in Alexandria.

In Measurement of a Circle he used the method of exhaustion to show that a circle has the same area as a right triangle whose base and height equal its radius and circumference, and he bounded pi by polygons of 96 sides, finding it between 3 10/71 and 3 1/7. In Quadrature of the Parabola he proved that the area enclosed by a parabola and a straight line is 4/3 of that of a corresponding inscribed triangle. In On the Equilibrium of Planes he proves the law of the lever.

Archimedes died during the siege of Syracuse, killed by a Roman soldier despite orders that he should not be harmed. Cicero describes visiting his tomb, surmounted by a sphere and a cylinder that he had asked to have placed there. His mathematical writings were little known in antiquity. The first comprehensive compilation was made around 530 CE by Isidore of Miletus in Constantinople, and his work was later translated into Arabic and then into Latin. The first printed edition appeared at Basel in 1544.
argead-dynasty: The dynasty, also called Temenid, had King Caranus as its mythical founder. Herodotus tells in The Histories that three brothers of the lineage of Temenus, named Gauanes, Aeropus and Perdiccas, fled from Argos to the Illyrians and then to a town called Lebaea in Upper Macedonia, where they served the king. Dismissed by him because of an omen that something great would happen to Perdiccas, they settled near the garden of Midas below Mount Bermio and slowly formed a kingdom of their own. A Greek inscription relating to the belief in descent from Heracles was found by Manolis Andronikos in the royal palace of Aigai, near modern Vergina.

According to Thucydides, in the History of the Peloponnesian War, the Argeads came down from the highlands to Lower Macedonia, expelled the Pierians from Pieria, gained a narrow strip along the river Axios reaching to Pella and the sea, and added Mygdonia by driving out the Edoni, Eordians and Almopians. Another theory, held by the Greek historian Miltiades Hatzopoulos following the ancient author Appian, is that the dynasty came from Argos Orestikon rather than from the Peloponnese, its people completing their wandering from Orestis to Lower Macedonia in the 7th century BCE.

The Argeads were at first rulers of the tribe of the same name, which prevailed in early Emathia, later Lower Macedonia, with its capital at Aigai. Herodotus relates that when Alexander I of Macedon entered the Olympic Games, in 504 or 500 BCE, other competitors objected that he was not Greek; the judges, the Hellanodikai, examined his Argead claim and allowed him to take part. By the time of Philip II of Macedon the kingdom, now governed from Pella, included all the states of Upper Macedonia.

The death of a king almost invariably set off disputes among members of the family, and often a war of succession. A six-year interregnum from 399 to 393 BCE followed the death of King Archelaus, and wars of succession followed the deaths of Pausanias, Amyntas III and Perdiccas III, the last of which brought Philip II to power in 360 to 359 BCE after he deposed Amyntas IV. An established king could also face rebellion by a relative, as Perdiccas II did from his brother Philip. Modern historians disagree on a number of details of the family's genealogy.
argentina: Argentina covers a mainland area of about 2,780,400 square kilometres in southern South America, sharing borders with Chile across the Andes, Bolivia, Paraguay, Brazil and Uruguay. The highest point is Aconcagua, in Mendoza province, at 6,959 metres above sea level, the highest in the Southern and Western Hemispheres. The maximum north–south distance is 3,694 kilometres. Its major rivers, among them the Paraná and the Uruguay, which join to form the Río de la Plata, discharge into the Argentine Sea over the Patagonian Shelf. It is one of the most biodiverse countries in the world, with 15 continental zones, 2 marine zones and the Antarctic region.
Humans inhabited the region as early as 21,000 years ago, and the Cueva de las Manos, in Santa Cruz, holds stencilled handprints and hunting scenes made between 7,300 BCE and 700 CE.

Before European colonisation Argentina was sparsely populated by diverse cultures: basic hunters and gatherers such as the Selkʼnam and Yahgan in the extreme south, more advanced hunters such as the Tehuelche, and farmers with pottery such as the Guaraní in the northeast and the Diaguita in the northwest, whom the Inca Empire conquered around 1480. Europeans first arrived with the 1502 voyage of Amerigo Vespucci. Pedro de Mendoza founded Buenos Aires in 1536, but it was abandoned in 1541, and Juan de Garay re-founded it in 1580.

Argentina rose as the successor state of the Viceroyalty of the Río de la Plata, founded in 1776. The Argentine War of Independence (1810–1825) and the Declaration of Independence of 9 July 1816 were followed by an extended civil war that lasted until 1880 and ended in reorganisation as a federation. The name Argentina comes from the Latin argentum, silver, after the silver mountains legend among early explorers. Later came relative peace and mass waves of millions of European immigrants, mainly Italians and Spaniards, who greatly influenced its culture and demography.

The National Autonomist Party dominated politics from 1880 until the 1916 elections. The first coup, in 1930, began the Infamous Decade, and between 1930 and 1976 the armed forces overthrew six governments. The final coup, in 1976, was followed by a military junta that persecuted and murdered thousands of political critics in the Dirty War, which lasted until Raúl Alfonsín was elected president in 1983. Argentina is a federal constitutional republic of twenty-three provinces and one autonomous city, Buenos Aires. The 2022 census counted 46,044,703 inhabitants, and 92% live in cities.
aristotle: The details of Aristotle's life are not well established, and ancient biographies are often speculative. He was born in 384 BCE in Stagira in Chalcidice, the son of Nicomachus, personal physician to King Amyntas of Macedon, and of Phaestis. His father was probably responsible for his early interest in biology and medicine. Both parents died while he was young, and Proxenus of Atarneus became his guardian.

At seventeen or eighteen Aristotle moved to Athens to study at Plato's Academy, where Plato called him the mind of the school. He stayed for nearly twenty years and left in 348 or 347 BCE after Plato's death. The traditional story is that he was disappointed when control passed to Plato's nephew Speusippus, though anti-Macedonian feeling in Athens may also have played a part. He went to Assos in Asia Minor at the invitation of Hermias of Atarneus, did research in botany and marine biology there with Theophrastus, and married Pythias, Hermias's adoptive daughter and niece.

Aristotle founded the Peripatetic school in the Lyceum in Athens and established a library there. Only around a third of his original output has survived, and most of it was probably edited by students and later lecturers. His logical works were compiled into the Organon around 40 BCE, and the Prior Analytics is credited with the earliest systematic study of logic.

In physics he added the heavenly aether to the four elements proposed by Empedocles. In ethics, as a virtue ethicist, he held that the aim of human action is eudaimonia, generally translated as happiness. In the Politics he treated the city as a natural community prior to the family and the individual, and stated that man is by nature a political animal.

At the request of Philip II of Macedon, Aristotle tutored Philip's son Alexander the Great from 343 BCE. His influence shaped medieval scholarship: Muslim scholars called him The First Teacher, and Christians such as Thomas Aquinas called him The Philosopher. His physical science was not replaced systematically until the Enlightenment.

His successor Theophrastus wrote the History of Plants, a pioneering work in botany. According to the philosopher Bryan Magee, it is doubtful whether any human being has ever known as much as Aristotle did.
armenia: The modern Republic of Armenia is a landlocked country in the Armenian highlands of West Asia, in the South Caucasus. It borders Turkey to the west, Georgia to the north, Azerbaijan to the east, and Iran and the Azerbaijani exclave of Nakhchivan to the south. Its area is 29,743 square kilometres. The terrain is mostly mountainous, with fast-flowing rivers and few forests, and 85.9% of the country is mountain area.

Mount Aragats rises to 4,090 metres. Mount Ararat, at 5,137 metres, was historically part of Armenia and is now in Turkey, but is clearly visible from Armenia. Armenians regard it as a symbol of their land, and it appears on the national emblem.

Acheulean tools more than a million years old mark the first human traces, and thousands of artefacts about 325,000 years old were found at Nor Geghi 1. Early civilisation dates to about 4000 BCE. Excavations at the Areni-1 cave complex in 2010 and 2011 uncovered the world's earliest known leather shoe, skirt and wine-producing facility. Bronze Age cultures and states included the Trialeti-Vanadzor culture, Hayasa-Azzi and Mitanni, followed by the Nairi confederation and its successor Urartu. A cuneiform inscription indicates that Yerevan was founded in the summer of 782 BCE by King Argishti I.

The exonym Armenia appears as Armina in the Old Persian Behistun Inscription of 515 BCE. The Kingdom of Armenia reached its height under Tigranes the Great in the 1st century BCE and adopted Christianity as its official religion in 301 CE. The Bagratid Kingdom of Armenia, restored in the 9th century, fell in 1045, and Cilician Armenia lay on the Mediterranean coast between the 11th and 14th centuries. Up to 1.5 million Armenians were exterminated in the Armenian genocide during World War I.

Armenia is a representative parliamentary democratic republic. It followed a semi-presidential model until April 2018, and the National Assembly is a unicameral parliament of 105 members. The country is divided into ten provinces, with Yerevan having special status. Its population was 3,081,100 in 2025, down from a peak of 3.6 million in 1991. The diaspora is estimated at 8 million by some counts, far larger than the population in Armenia, with the largest communities in Russia, the United States and France.
asaf-ud-daula: Born on 23 September 1748, Asaf-ud-Daula was the son of Shuja-ud-Daula and of Umat-ul-Zohra, better known as Bahu Begum. He became nawab at the age of 26 on his father's death in January 1775, with the aid of the British East India Company. His younger brother Saadat Ali led a mutiny in the army, which the British Colonel John Parker defeated decisively. Asaf's first chief minister, Mukhtar-ud-Daula, was assassinated in the revolt. His position as Nawab wazir was ratified by the Mughal emperor Shah Alam II.

After the revolt he restructured the government, appointing nobles favourable to him and British officers to his army. Hasan Riza Khan became chief minister, ably assisted by Haydar Beg Khan, and Tikayt Ray finance minister. His mother remained a challenge to his rule: she controlled much of the treasury, held her own jagirs and armed forces, and at one point sought the Company's help in appointing ministers opposed to him.

Shuja-ud-Daula had left two million pounds sterling in the vaults of the zenana, which his widow and his mother claimed under a will that was never produced. When Warren Hastings pressed the nawab for the debt due to the Company, Asaf obtained from his mother a loan of 26 lakh rupees against a jagir of four times the value, and later 30 lakh more in return for a full acquittal and the Company's recognition of her jagirs for life. The jagirs were afterwards confiscated on the ground of her complicity in the rising of Chait Singh.

The Bara Imambara, or Asafi Imambara, was begun as a charitable project to give employment in the famine of 1784, in which even nobles were reduced to penury. It is said that over 20,000 people worked on it, and that nobles were paid to pull down part of the work in secret at night so that their dignity was kept. The Rumi Darwaza, sixty feet tall, was modelled in 1784 on the Sublime Porte in Istanbul.

He died in Lucknow on 21 September 1797 and is buried at the Bara Imambara. A saying still known in the city records his generosity: to whom even God does not give, Asaf-ud-Daula gives. The painter Johann Zoffany portrayed him several times, and the Urdu poet Mir Taqi Mir was at his court.
asia: Asia holds roughly 60% of the world's population. It shares the landmass of Eurasia with Europe, and its border with Europe is a historical and cultural construct, as there is no clear physical separation between them. Greek geographers such as Anaximander and Hecataeus used a threefold division of the Old World from the 6th century BCE, and the Ural River prevailed as the boundary in the mid-19th century. The boundary with Africa is the Suez Canal, the Gulf of Suez, the Red Sea and the Bab-el-Mandeb. Asia has the longest coastline of any continent, at 62,800 kilometres.

Researchers believe modern humans migrated to South Asia along the Indian Ocean about 60,000 years ago, and that they interbred with Denisovans in Southeast Asia. The history of Asia can be seen as the distinct histories of several peripheral coastal regions, East Asia, South Asia, Southeast Asia, Central Asia and West Asia.

The coastal periphery was home to some of the world's earliest known civilisations, each developing around fertile river valleys: those of Mesopotamia, the Indus Valley and the Yellow River shared many similarities and may have exchanged technologies and ideas such as mathematics and the wheel, while writing seems to have developed independently in each area.

Evidence of farming in West Asia dates back to around 9000 BCE. China and India traded places as the largest economies in the world from 1 to 1800 CE, and the Silk Road became the main east–west trading route in the Asian hinterlands, while the Straits of Malacca stood as a major sea route. Asia was the birthplace of most of the world's mainstream religions, including Islam, Judaism, Christianity, Hinduism and Buddhism.

Asia is subdivided into 49 countries, five of them transcontinental (Georgia, Azerbaijan, Russia, Kazakhstan and Turkey). The United Nations Statistics Division divides it into North Asia, Central Asia, West Asia, South Asia, East Asia and Southeast Asia, solely for statistical reasons. It has no single culture: various independent cultures coexist, and it varies greatly in ethnic groups, environments, economies and government systems. Asia is home to several language families, and more than 700 languages are spoken in Indonesia, over 400 in India and more than 100 in the Philippines.
athens: Athens spreads across the central plain of Attica, the Athens Basin, which is bounded by Mount Aigaleo to the west, Mount Parnitha to the north, Mount Pentelicus to the north-east and Mount Hymettus to the east. The Saronic Gulf lies to the south-west. Lycabettus is one of the tallest of the many hills of the city. Ancient writers debated whether the city took its name from the goddess Athena or she from it, and modern scholars generally agree that the goddess took her name from the city. In the founding myth Athena and Poseidon competed for patronage of the city, and Athena won by offering the first olive tree.

The oldest known human presence is in the Cave of Schist, dated between the 11th and 7th millennia BCE, and Athens has been inhabited continuously for at least 5,000 years. By 1400 BCE it was an important Mycenaean centre, with a major fortress on the Acropolis. It is not known whether Athens was destroyed around 1200 BCE, as other Mycenaean centres were, and the Athenians always held that they were pure Ionians. After about 150 years of economic decline, its richly furnished Iron Age burials show that from 900 BCE it was again one of the leading centres of trade in the region.

Classical Athens was one of the most powerful city-states of ancient Greece and a centre of democracy, the arts, education and philosophy. It influenced the Hellenistic world and, above all, ancient Rome. Its chronology runs through Roman rule from 86 BCE, the Byzantine Empire from 395, the Duchy of Athens from 1205 to 1458, Ottoman rule from 1458 and Greece from 1833. Athens became the capital in 1834, after Nafplion, the provisional capital from 1829.

Athens is the capital and largest city of Greece and the capital of the Attica region. The monuments of the Classical age are still visible, the best known being the Parthenon, and the city also keeps Roman, Byzantine and a few Ottoman monuments. The Acropolis of Athens and the medieval Daphni Monastery are UNESCO World Heritage Sites. Athens hosted the first modern Olympic Games in 1896 and the Summer Olympics again in 2004.
atlantic-ocean: The Atlantic is the second largest of the world's five oceans, with an area of about 85,133,000 square kilometres, roughly 17% of Earth's surface. It occupies an elongated, S-shaped basin between Europe and Africa to the east and the Americas to the west. It connects to the Arctic Ocean in the north, the Pacific in the southwest, the Indian Ocean in the southeast along the 20° East meridian, and the Southern Ocean in the south. The Equator divides it into northern and southern parts.

A submarine mountain range, the Mid-Atlantic Ridge, runs down its length from 87°N to Bouvet Island at 54°S and divides it into two halves. It marks the boundary between the North American and Eurasian plates and between the South American and African plates. The break-up of Pangaea began in the central Atlantic, between North America and Northwest Africa, in the Late Triassic and Early Jurassic. The Gulf Stream and the North Atlantic Drift help keep the British Isles and northwestern Europe mild in winter.

The oldest known mentions of an Atlantic sea come from Stesichorus around the mid-sixth century BCE and from Herodotus around 450 BCE, where the name refers to the sea beyond the Pillars of Hercules, named for the Titan Atlas. Early Greek sailors believed it to be part of Oceanus, the great sea or river that surrounds all land. The southern Atlantic was called the Aethiopian Ocean as late as the mid-19th century, and English cartographers of the Age of Discovery called it the Great Western Ocean.

The Norse were the first known humans to cross the ocean, but the expedition of Christopher Columbus in 1492 proved the most consequential. It began an age of exploration and colonisation of the Americas by European powers, most notably Portugal, Spain, France and the United Kingdom.

From the 16th to the 19th centuries the Atlantic was the centre of the Atlantic slave trade and the Columbian exchange, and it occasionally hosted naval battles. Such battles and the growing trade of American powers such as the United States and Brazil increased in the early 20th century. Notable postwar conflicts include the Cuban Missile Crisis and the Falklands War.

The ocean remains a core component of trade around the world, with major transatlantic transport and communication routes. Its continental shelves hold petroleum and gas fields. They also include some of the world's richest fishing grounds, among them the Grand Banks of Newfoundland, Georges Bank and the Dogger Bank of the North Sea. Its marginal seas include the Mediterranean, the Baltic, the North Sea, the Caribbean and the Gulf of Mexico.
australia: Australia comprises the mainland of the Australian continent, the island of Tasmania and numerous smaller islands. It has a land area of 7,688,287 square kilometres, the sixth largest in the world, and the mainland is the world's smallest continent. About 70% of the landmass is arid or semi-arid, and the mainland is relatively flat. The Great Dividing Range runs along most of the east, and Mount Kosciuszko, at 2,228 metres, is the highest mountain on the mainland. The Murray-Darling is the major river system. The Great Barrier Reef, the world's largest coral reef, lies off the north-east coast and extends for more than 2,300 kilometres.

Human habitation is estimated to have begun 50,000 to 65,000 years ago, with migration from what is now Southeast Asia. Aboriginal Australian culture is one of the oldest continuous cultures on Earth. At first European contact Aboriginal Australians belonged to a wide range of societies across at least 250 language groups, and estimates of their population before British settlement range from 300,000 to 3 million. Torres Strait Islander people first settled their islands at least 2,500 years ago and are culturally and linguistically distinct from mainland peoples. Trade had been established by the mid-18th century between Aboriginal groups in the north and Makassan trepangers visiting from present-day Indonesia.

In 1606 the crew of the Dutch ship Duyfken, captained by Willem Janszoon, made the first documented European landing. Abel Tasman's voyage of 1642 was the first known European expedition to reach Van Diemen's Land, and the Dutch named the continent New Holland. British colonisation began in 1788 with the penal colony of New South Wales. Governor Lachlan Macquarie recommended the name Australia in December 1817. By 1890 each of six self-governing colonies had gained responsible government, and they federated in 1901 as the Commonwealth of Australia. The Australia Act 1986 completed the process of increasing autonomy from the United Kingdom.

Australia has a population of 27,801,023, heavily concentrated on the east coast and highly urbanised, with Canberra as capital and Sydney and Melbourne as the most populous cities. It is a constitutional monarchy, a parliamentary democracy and a federation of six states and ten territories, with a constitution mostly unchanged since 1901. The white Australia policy, strengthened after Federation, ended in 1973, and immigrants now account for 30% of the population. Indigenous art includes more than 100,000 Aboriginal rock art sites.
austria: Austria is a landlocked country in Central Europe, lying in the Eastern Alps, and occupies 83,879 square kilometres. Only about a quarter of its area can be considered low-lying, and only 32% of the country lies below 500 metres. The Eastern Alps make up 62% of the total area, and the Alps of the west give way to lowlands and plains in the east. The Austrian granite plateau, part of the Bohemian Mass, accounts for 10%, and forest covers about 47% of the land. It is a federation of nine states, of which Vienna is the most populous.

By the 6th century BCE the region was settled by Celtic tribes and served as the core of the Hallstatt culture; the city of Hallstatt has the oldest archaeological evidence of the Celts in Europe. The Celtic Kingdom of Noricum was conquered by the Roman Empire in 16 BCE and lasted as a province until 476, while eastern parts fell in Pannonia and the west in Raetia.

Carnuntum, an army camp turned capital, was home to 50,000 people for nearly 400 years. After the fall of the Roman Empire, Odoacer conquered most of the area in 487, the Ostrogoths followed by 493, and the Alemanni, Baiuvarii, Slavs and Avars after them. Charlemagne defeated the Avars in the late eighth century and set up frontier marches.

In 976 Emperor Otto II appointed Leopold I of the House of Babenberg as margrave of the marchia Orientalis. The name Austria first appears in writing in 996, as Ostarrîchi. The Privilegium Minus made Austria a duchy in 1156, and the Babenbergs acquired Styria in 1192; the line ended with Frederick II in 1246. Ottokar II of Bohemia then took control of the duchies until Rudolph I of Germany defeated him at Dürnkrut in 1278. From then until the First World War, Austria's history was largely that of the Habsburgs, and it became an archduchy in 1453.

Austria had established its own empire two years before the dissolution of the Holy Roman Empire in 1806, and Austria-Hungary followed in 1867. The empire's defeat in the First World War led to the Republic of German-Austria in 1918 and the First Austrian Republic in 1919. An Austrofascist dictatorship under Engelbert Dollfuss formed in 1934, and Nazi Germany annexed the country a year before the Second World War.

After liberation in 1945 and a decade of Allied occupation, Austria regained its sovereignty and declared perpetual neutrality in 1955. It joined the European Union in 1995 and adopted the euro in 1999; its population was estimated at 9,220,882 in April 2026, and Vienna exceeds 2 million.
az-zahir-ghazi: Al-Malik az-Zahir Ghiyath ud-din Ghazi was the third son of Saladin. In 1186, when he was 15, his father appointed him governor of Aleppo, Mosul and the neighbouring areas recently taken from the Zengids, lands that had been under the control of Saladin's brother al-Adil. His two older brothers received Syria (al-Afdal) and Egypt (al-Aziz) at the same time. When he inherited in 1193 he was to owe suzerainty to al-Afdal in Damascus, but he conducted his affairs independently and for a while stayed out of his brothers' quarrels with their uncle.

In 1193 he called on al-Adil for troops to put down the revolt of the Zengid Izz al-Din in Mosul. The next year he received Latakia and Jableh in a settlement by which he recognised al-Afdal's authority, but in 1196 he joined al-Aziz and al-Adil in deposing and exiling that brother. In October 1197, with Bohemond III of Antioch threatening Latakia and Jableh, he destroyed the two ports; Bohemond took them, found them of no use and withdrew, and az-Zahir reoccupied them and rebuilt the fortress at Latakia. He kept many of his father's advisers and appointed Baha ad-Din as a judge in Aleppo.

After al-Aziz died in 1198, az-Zahir allied with al-Afdal, and with most of the other Ayyubid princes they besieged Damascus. The city held out for months, and he withdrew his troops. Al-Adil, having conquered Egypt, returned, reduced az-Zahir's territories to the area around Aleppo and forced him to recognise his suzerainty. In his last decade az-Zahir skirmished with crusaders and lent his army to other Ayyubid princes. King Leo of Cilicia defeated his forces at the Battle of Amq in 1206 but gained no lasting advantage against Aleppo, and in 1207 his troops lifted a siege of Homs.

In 1212 az-Zahir married Dayfa Khatun, the daughter of his old rival al-Adil, a match that ended the rivalry between the two branches of the family. Before his death he appointed his younger son al-Aziz Muhammad, born in 1213, to succeed him. He died on 8 October 1216. His lands had included northern Syria and a small part of Mesopotamia.
azerbaijan: The name Azerbaijan derives from Atropates, a Persian satrap under the Achaemenid Empire who was reinstated as satrap of Media under Alexander the Great; the Greek name is a transliteration of an Old Iranian, probably Median, name meaning protected by the holy fire or the land of the holy fire. It evolved through Middle Persian Āturpātākān to the present form. The name was first adopted by the government of Musavat in 1918, when the independent Azerbaijan Democratic Republic was established. Until then the name designated the adjacent region of northwestern Iran, while the republic's area had been called Arran and Shirvan, and Iran protested.

The earliest evidence of human settlement dates to the late Stone Age and is related to the Guruchay culture of Azykh Cave. The Scythians settled in the 9th century BCE, and the Iranian Medes came to dominate the area south of the Aras river before it was integrated into the Achaemenid Empire around 550 BCE, which spread Zoroastrianism. The Sasanian Empire turned Caucasian Albania into a vassal state in 252, and King Urnayr adopted Christianity as the state religion in the 4th century.

In the first half of the 7th century Albania came under nominal Muslim rule, and the Umayyad Caliphate made it a vassal state after suppressing Christian resistance led by King Juansher in 667. Oghuz Turks seized the territory from the beginning of the 11th century, and the Seljuk Empire entered the area by 1067; under the Seljuks poets such as Nizami Ganjavi and Khaqani gave rise to a blossoming of Persian literature.

Until the 19th century the region remained part of Qajar Iran. The Russo-Persian wars of 1804–1813 and 1826–1828 forced the Qajar Empire to cede its Caucasian territories to the Russian Empire, and the treaties of Gulistan in 1813 and Turkmenchay in 1828 defined the border between Russia and Iran. An Azerbaijani national identity emerged by the late 19th century. The Azerbaijan Democratic Republic, proclaimed in 1918, became the first secular democratic Muslim-majority state in the world, and in 1920 the country was conquered and incorporated into the Soviet Union.

The modern Republic of Azerbaijan proclaimed its independence on 30 August 1991. The Nagorno-Karabakh region became de facto independent as the Republic of Artsakh with the end of the First Nagorno-Karabakh War in 1994. Azerbaijan is a unitary semi-presidential republic. About 97% of its 10,164,464 people are Muslim, and 94.8% are Azerbaijanis.
